fastQR: factorization, updating and statistical applications

Mauro Bernardi, Claudio Busatto and Manuela Cattelan

16 November 2026

A QR factorization provides a numerical representation that can be reused across estimation, prediction and changes to the data. This guide develops that idea from the construction of the factors to sliding-window regression and ridge model selection. The mathematical discussion explains what each representation retains, while the R examples examine both its numerical accuracy and the work required to compute or update it.

1 From a matrix to a verified QR factorization

A design matrix often appears in several related calculations: estimating coefficients, producing predictions, adding observations or changing the set of predictors. A QR factorization records its geometry in a form that can support each of these operations. Understanding what the factors contain is therefore useful before deciding whether to store an explicit orthogonal basis, retain only a triangular factor or keep the orthogonal transformations in compact form.

This chapter introduces those representations through the identities they satisfy. The examples check reconstruction and orthogonality separately, then examine the column-ordering convention used by pivoted QR. These checks provide a common basis for the update and regression examples that follow.

The examples use fastQR 1.1.6, ggplot2 for figures and knitr for tables. All code uses explicit fastQR:: or base:: namespaces because both packages export a function named qr. For the examples in this guide, use the accompanying verified source build described on the Overview page. No attachment with library(fastQR) is required below.

1.1 Full, thin and compact representations

Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) have full column rank, with \(n>p\). Its thin factorization is \[ X=Q_1R_1,\qquad Q_1^\top Q_1=I_p, \] where \(Q_1\) is \(n\times p\) and \(R_1\) is nonsingular, upper triangular and \(p\times p\). The columns of \(Q_1\) are orthonormal; \(Q_1Q_1^\top\) is a projector and need not equal \(I_n\).

The full factorization completes \(Q_1\) to an orthogonal matrix by adding \(n-p\) orthonormal columns: \[ \begin{aligned} Q&=[Q_1,Q_2]\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, & Q_2&\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-p)},\\ R&=\begin{pmatrix}R_1\\0_{(n-p)\times p}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}, & X&=QR=Q_1R_1. \end{aligned} \] Here \(Q_1^\top Q_2=0_{p\times(n-p)}\) and \(Q_2^\top Q_2=I_{n-p}\), so \(Q_2\) spans the orthogonal complement of the column space of \(X\). The zero block in \(R\) contributes nothing to the product; the thin representation therefore suffices to reconstruct \(X\).

The orthogonal complement is needed for some operations on complete factors, but it contributes nothing to the reconstruction of the original design. Its storage can be substantial when \(n\) is much larger than \(p\), which motivates retaining the thin factors whenever the subsequent calculation permits it. A compact representation goes a step further by storing the Householder transformations that define Q and forming its columns only when requested.

The triangular factor \(R_1\) should also be distinguished from the symmetric cross-product matrix. An upper triangular matrix is not generally symmetric or positive definite; under full column rank, the positive-definite matrix is \(R_1^\top R_1=X^\top X\).

Task Function Representation
Work directly with \(Q\) and \(R\) fastQR::qr() Explicit factors; full or thin
Store Householder information compactly fastQR::qr_fast() Packed factorization, optionally pivoted
Extract factors from packed output qr_Q(), qr_R() Form only the factors needed
Retain a triangular factor only qrchol(), rchol() \(R\) satisfying \(R^\top R=X^\top X\)

1.1.1 Rank and rectangular shapes

The factorization identity itself does not require a unique least-squares coefficient vector. If a design has dependent columns, a triangular factor can still represent it, but solving an unpivoted triangular system with a zero diagonal is no longer the full-column-rank calculation derived above. A rank-revealing pivoted factorization separates that situation from an ordinary full-rank solve.

A wide design with \(p>n\) also admits an orthogonal factorization, with Q of size \(n\times n\) and R of size \(n\times p\). It cannot have full column rank, so its unpenalized coefficient vector is not uniquely determined by the fitted response. The qr() and compact qr_fast() interfaces support that representation; the thin-factor interface has a different input contract. Ordinary least-squares interfaces retain their full-column-rank restrictions. Positive-penalty ridge fits also support wide designs; the chapter on ridge with growing designs develops this case through augmented least squares.

The declared numerical rank and the number of stored Householder transformations also serve different purposes. Extraction through qr_Q() and qr_R() follows their documented rank-dependent output rule. qr_Q_full() constructs the complete orthogonal transformation from the compact information when that full transformation is required.

1.2 A first reproducible example

We generate a modest, full-rank design so that the dimensions and checks are easy to inspect. complete = FALSE avoids constructing an unnecessary \(n\times n\) matrix.

set.seed(2026)
n <- 120L
p <- 6L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
thin <- fastQR::qr(X, type = "householder", complete = FALSE)
full <- fastQR::qr(X, type = "householder", complete = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  representation = c("Thin", "Full"),
  Q_rows = c(nrow(thin$Q), nrow(full$Q)),
  Q_columns = c(ncol(thin$Q), ncol(full$Q)),
  R_rows = c(nrow(thin$R), nrow(full$R)),
  R_columns = c(ncol(thin$R), ncol(full$R))))
representation Q_rows Q_columns R_rows R_columns
Thin 120 6 6 6
Full 120 120 120 6

The factorization has two distinct defining properties: multiplication of the factors reconstructs X, and the columns of Q have the required inner products. The checks below examine both properties. The full Q is compared with \(I_n\) through \(Q^\top Q\), whereas the thin Q is compared with \(I_p\) through \(Q_1^\top Q_1\). These different identity sizes are a direct consequence of the dimensions of the two representations.

The helper scales a matrix difference by the Frobenius norm of its reference. This makes discrepancies comparable across matrices with different overall magnitudes. Its denominator is bounded below by machine epsilon to avoid division by zero; for the nonzero reference matrices in this example it is the usual relative error. The same helper is reused when the design is updated.

relative_error <- function(actual, reference) {
  norm(as.matrix(actual - reference), "F") /
    max(norm(as.matrix(reference), "F"), .Machine$double.eps)
}
checks <- c(
  thin_reconstruction = relative_error(thin$Q %*% thin$R, X),
  full_reconstruction = relative_error(full$Q %*% full$R, X),
  thin_orthogonality = relative_error(crossprod(thin$Q), diag(p)),
  full_orthogonality = relative_error(crossprod(full$Q), diag(n)),
  Gram_identity = relative_error(crossprod(thin$R), crossprod(X)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(check = names(checks), relative_error = unname(checks)),
             digits = 16)
check relative_error
thin_reconstruction 2e-16
full_reconstruction 4e-16
thin_orthogonality 1e-16
full_orthogonality 4e-16
Gram_identity 2e-16 
stopifnot(max(checks) < 1e-10)

These are checks of the defining identities. Comparing two implementations’ entries of \(Q\) and \(R\) directly would be misleading: paired column/row sign changes can produce equally valid factors.

1.2.1 Recovering a least-squares coefficient vector

Once the thin factors are available, the response enters through its projection onto the columns of Q. For a response \(y\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(c=Q_1^\top y\). The least-squares coefficient vector satisfies \(R_1\widehat\beta=c\), so a complete calculation needs a matrix-vector product followed by a triangular solve. Writing \(R_1^{-1}c\) is a mathematical identity, but an implementation can obtain the result without constructing an inverse.

The following response combines a linear signal with a deterministic perturbation. The perturbation makes the residual nonzero, allowing us to check its orthogonality to the fitted column space as well as the coefficient calculation. It is a numerical example, rather than a simulation of a particular observation-noise model.

demo_y <- drop(X %*% seq_len(p)) + sin(seq_len(n))
demo_projection <- crossprod(thin$Q, demo_y)
demo_coefficients <- backsolve(thin$R, demo_projection)
demo_fitted <- drop(X %*% demo_coefficients)
demo_residuals <- demo_y - demo_fitted
qr_derivation_checks <- c(
  coefficient_agreement = max(abs(demo_coefficients - lm.fit(X, demo_y)$coefficients)),
  fitted_projection = relative_error(demo_fitted, thin$Q %*% demo_projection),
  residual_orthogonality = max(abs(crossprod(thin$Q, demo_residuals))) /
    max(1, sqrt(sum(demo_y^2))))
stopifnot(max(qr_derivation_checks) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(check = names(qr_derivation_checks),
                        error = unname(qr_derivation_checks)), digits = 12)
check error
coefficient_agreement 0
fitted_projection 0
residual_orthogonality 0

The response projection has p entries, whereas the fitted response and residual have n. Multiplication by the thin Q maps between those coordinate systems. The near-zero value of \(Q_1^\top e\) verifies the defining least-squares geometry, while comparison with lm.fit() checks the resulting coefficients against a separate implementation.

1.3 Pivoting: keep track of the column order

Column pivoting changes the order in which the columns are factorized. With the permutation matrix returned by qr_pivot2perm(), the convention used here is \[ X=QRP,\qquad XP^\top=QR. \] Thus the correct Gram check is \(R^\top R=PX^\top XP^\top\), not generally \(R^\top R=X^\top X\).

Pivoting also changes the coordinates of the coefficient vector. If \(z=P\beta\), then \(X\beta=QRz\). The triangular solve therefore returns \(\widehat z\) in pivoted order; the original predictor order is recovered by \(\widehat\beta=P^\top\widehat z\). Restoring that order is necessary before interpreting individual coefficients or multiplying them by an unpermuted prediction design.

packed <- fastQR::qr_fast(X, pivot = TRUE)
Q <- fastQR::qr_Q(packed$qr, tau = packed$qraux,
                  rank = packed$rank, complete = FALSE)
R <- fastQR::qr_R(packed$qr, rank = NULL, complete = FALSE)
P <- fastQR::qr_pivot2perm(packed$pivot)
pivot_checks <- c(
  reconstruction = relative_error(Q %*% R %*% P, X),
  permuted_Gram = relative_error(crossprod(R), crossprod(X %*% t(P))))
knitr::kable(data.frame(check = names(pivot_checks), error = pivot_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)
check error
reconstruction 2e-16
permuted_Gram 1e-16 
stopifnot(max(pivot_checks) < 1e-10)
pivoted_coefficients <- backsolve(R, crossprod(Q, demo_y))
original_order_coefficients <- drop(t(P) %*% pivoted_coefficients)
pivot_derivation_error <- max(abs(original_order_coefficients - demo_coefficients))
stopifnot(pivot_derivation_error < 1e-10)

All subsequent update examples start from unpivoted factors, so that insertion and deletion positions refer directly to the original columns. Rank-deficient designs require additional care; the worked examples retain full column rank.

1.4 Triangular factors and linear systems

A triangular factor can be useful even when the subsequent calculation does not require an explicit orthogonal basis. The identity \(R^\top R=X^\top X\) provides the cross-product information through R, with storage proportional to \(p^2\). Two valid factors can have different row signs while satisfying the same identity, so agreement of the invariant is more informative here than equality of their entries.

The final part of the example solves a square system \(Au=b\), where \(A=X^\top X+I_p\). In this call, qrsolve(A, b) factorizes A and solves for u. It is distinct from directly computing least-squares coefficients by factorizing X and projecting a response. Adding the identity makes this demonstration system positive definite; its purpose is to show the solver interface on an easily checked calculation.

R_qr <- fastQR::qrchol(X)
R_only <- fastQR::rchol(X)
stopifnot(relative_error(crossprod(R_qr), crossprod(X)) < 1e-10,
          relative_error(crossprod(R_only), crossprod(X)) < 1e-10)

A <- crossprod(X) + diag(p)
b <- seq_len(p)
solution <- fastQR::qrsolve(A, b, type = "QR")
relative_error(A %*% solution, b)
## [1] 6.092069e-16
stopifnot(relative_error(A %*% solution, b) < 1e-10)

The square system above is deliberately well conditioned. Later examples distinguish factorization error from the sensitivity of a least-squares solution to an ill-conditioned design.

2 Updating a factorization as the data change

Many statistical calculations involve a sequence of designs that differ by only a few observations or predictors. A moving-window analysis, for example, repeatedly removes the oldest observation and includes a new one. Recomputing a factorization at every step repeats work on the part of the design that has not changed.

Updating and downdating use the existing factors to incorporate that local change. The choice of representation remains important: qrupdate() and qrdowndate() modify QR factors, whereas rupdate() and rdowndate() retain only the triangular information. The examples first examine individual insertions and deletions, where the resulting design is easy to reconstruct, before combining the operations in a repeated regression calculation.

2.1 Insert and remove observations

We use full factors as inputs to the QR update routines in these examples. A batch containing \(m\) new rows is supplied as a \(p\times m\) matrix U: its transpose is appended to the design. The position k is one-based; k = n + 1 appends observations.

set.seed(2027)
n <- 120L
p <- 6L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
initial <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = TRUE)
U <- matrix(rnorm(p * 3L), p, 3L)
X_added <- rbind(X, t(U))
added <- fastQR::qrupdate(
  Q = initial$Q, R = initial$R, k = n + 1L, U = U,
  type = "row", fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
removed <- fastQR::qrdowndate(
  Q = added$Q, R = added$R, k = n + 1L, m = ncol(U),
  type = "row", fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
relative_error <- function(a, b) {
  norm(as.matrix(a - b), "F") / max(norm(as.matrix(b), "F"), .Machine$double.eps)
}
row_checks <- c(
  after_insertion = relative_error(added$Q %*% added$R, X_added),
  after_deletion = relative_error(removed$Q %*% removed$R, X))
knitr::kable(data.frame(operation = names(row_checks), error = row_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)
operation error
after_insertion 4e-16
after_deletion 5e-16 
stopifnot(max(row_checks) < 1e-10)

Removing the same observations restores the original design, although it need not reproduce the original factor entries: signs and orthogonal completions can differ while representing the same matrix. Reconstruction therefore provides the relevant check. A downdated QR representation can also exist after a loss of rank, but a unique ordinary least-squares coefficient vector then requires additional treatment. The remaining design should be checked before its triangular factor is used in an unpivoted regression solve.

2.2 Insert and remove predictors

Adding a predictor changes the column space that a regression model can use. If V contains new columns, their components along the existing basis are \(Q_1^\top V\), while \((I_n-Q_1Q_1^\top)V\) contains directions not already represented by X. A column-update algorithm incorporates those components and restores a triangular factor for the enlarged design. If the residual directions are dependent, the enlarged matrix does not acquire one independent direction per new column.

The insertion position changes the order of the predictors, so reconstruction is checked against a design assembled in exactly that order. Column deletion reverses the structural change, but the returned factors need not have the same entries as the starting factors.

For columns, U has the same number of rows as the design. Here two new predictors are inserted before column 3 and then removed from those same positions.

V <- matrix(rnorm(n * 2L), n, 2L)
k <- 3L
X_wider <- cbind(X[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], V, X[, 3:p, drop = FALSE])
wider <- fastQR::qrupdate(
  initial$Q, initial$R, k = k, U = V, type = "column",
  fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
narrower <- fastQR::qrdowndate(
  wider$Q, wider$R, k = k, m = ncol(V), type = "column",
  fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
stopifnot(relative_error(wider$Q %*% wider$R, X_wider) < 1e-10,
          relative_error(narrower$Q %*% narrower$R, X) < 1e-10)

2.3 Update only the triangular factor

For new rows, the Gram identity becomes \[ X_{\mathrm{new}}^\top X_{\mathrm{new}}=X^\top X+UU^\top =R^\top R+UU^\top. \] rupdate() returns a new triangular factor satisfying this identity, without returning \(Q\). To delete those rows, rdowndate() takes their values in U rather than their positions.

For predictor insertion, the required cross-products have a different structure. Appending \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) gives \[ [X,V]^\top[X,V] =\begin{pmatrix}R^\top R&X^\top V\\V^\top X&V^\top V\end{pmatrix}. \] The old factor determines the upper-left block, but it does not contain the cross-products between X and the new predictors. This is why the R-only column-update interface also receives the design values. For row deletion, the values of the observations being removed determine the subtraction \(UU^\top\); their positions alone would not supply that information.

R_initial <- initial$R[seq_len(p), , drop = FALSE]
R_added <- fastQR::rupdate(X, R_initial, U = U, type = "row", fast = FALSE)
R_removed <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_added, U = U, type = "row", fast = FALSE)

# R-only column updates append new columns to the right.
R_wider <- fastQR::rupdate(X, R_initial, U = V, type = "column", fast = FALSE)
R_narrower <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_wider, k = p + 1L, m = ncol(V),
                               type = "column", fast = FALSE)
r_checks <- c(
  add_rows = relative_error(crossprod(R_added), crossprod(X_added)),
  remove_rows = relative_error(crossprod(R_removed), crossprod(X)),
  add_columns = relative_error(crossprod(R_wider), crossprod(cbind(X, V))),
  remove_columns = relative_error(crossprod(R_narrower), crossprod(X)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(operation = names(r_checks), error = r_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)
operation error
add_rows 3e-16
remove_rows 2e-16
add_columns 2e-16
remove_columns 2e-16 
stopifnot(max(r_checks) < 1e-10)

2.4 A sliding-window regression

A moving window provides a statistical example of repeated updating and downdating. At each step we discard the oldest observation and append a new one. In addition to \(R\), we maintain \(h=X^\top y\). The regression coefficient vector solves \[ R^\top z=h,\qquad R\widehat\beta=z. \] The first solve is lower triangular because it uses \(R^\top\); in R it is forwardsolve(t(R), h). The result is then passed to backsolve(R, ...). These are the two stages of solving \(R^\top R\widehat\beta=h\). Solving only \(R\widehat\beta=h\) would use a different system and would not recover the least-squares coefficients.

When one observation \((x_{\mathrm{old}}^\top,y_{\mathrm{old}})\) is removed and another is inserted, the response cross-product changes through \[ h_{\mathrm{new}} =h_{\mathrm{old}}-x_{\mathrm{old}}y_{\mathrm{old}} +x_{\mathrm{new}}y_{\mathrm{new}}. \] Here each x on the right is a p-dimensional column vector. The code stores the corresponding design rows, so crossprod(old_x, old_y) and crossprod(new_x, new_y) construct these contributions in the required shape. Maintaining h makes the updated triangular factor usable for regression without recomputing the full response cross-product.

The simulation below keeps 100 observations in the window and processes 30 replacements. An intercept is included explicitly. At every step we compare the updated solution with a fresh lm.fit() fit.

set.seed(2028)
window <- 100L
steps <- 30L
p <- 5L
X_stream <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm((window + steps) * (p - 1L)),
                            window + steps, p - 1L))
beta_true <- c(1, 2, -1, 0, .5)
y_stream <- drop(X_stream %*% beta_true + rnorm(window + steps, sd = .7))
X_window <- X_stream[seq_len(window), , drop = FALSE]
y_window <- y_stream[seq_len(window)]
R_window <- fastQR::qr(X_window, complete = FALSE)$R
h <- crossprod(X_window, y_window)
coef_update <- coef_fresh <- matrix(NA_real_, steps, p)
gram_error <- numeric(steps)
for (s in seq_len(steps)) {
  old_x <- X_window[1, , drop = FALSE]
  old_y <- y_window[1]
  new_x <- X_stream[window + s, , drop = FALSE]
  new_y <- y_stream[window + s]
  R_minus <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_window, U = t(old_x), type = "row")
  X_minus <- X_window[-1, , drop = FALSE]
  R_window <- fastQR::rupdate(X_minus, R_minus, U = t(new_x), type = "row")
  h <- h - crossprod(old_x, old_y) + crossprod(new_x, new_y)
  X_window <- rbind(X_minus, new_x)
  y_window <- c(y_window[-1], new_y)
  coef_update[s, ] <- backsolve(R_window, forwardsolve(t(R_window), h))
  coef_fresh[s, ] <- lm.fit(X_window, y_window)$coefficients
  gram_error[s] <- relative_error(crossprod(R_window), crossprod(X_window))
}
max_coefficient_error <- max(abs(coef_update - coef_fresh))
stopifnot(max_coefficient_error < 1e-9, max(gram_error) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  check = c("Maximum coefficient difference", "Maximum relative Gram error"),
  value = c(max_coefficient_error, max(gram_error))), digits = 16)
check value
Maximum coefficient difference 5.81e-14
Maximum relative Gram error 2.04e-14

The coefficient trajectories in Figure 1 show how the fitted model changes as observations enter and leave the window. Each updated trajectory is paired with a fresh least-squares fit on exactly the same observations. Their overlap checks the repeated-update calculation; variation along the horizontal axis reflects changes in the data window, rather than a different estimator.

path_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(step = rep(seq_len(steps), p), coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), each = steps)),
             estimate = as.vector(coef_update), method = "Updated factors"),
  data.frame(step = rep(seq_len(steps), p), coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), each = steps)),
             estimate = as.vector(coef_fresh), method = "Fresh fit"))
ggplot2::ggplot(path_data, ggplot2::aes(step, estimate, colour = coefficient,
                                      linetype = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Fresh fit" = "dashed", "Updated factors" = "solid")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Window replacement", y = "Coefficient estimate", colour = "Coefficient",
                linetype = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

Figure 1: Coefficient estimates as the window advances. Solid lines use updated factors; dashed lines are fresh least-squares fits. The two computations agree to numerical precision.

This example illustrates the algorithm, not a claim about universal speed or long-run stability. Over long sequences, monitor reconstruction or Gram errors and consider periodic refactorization. Maintaining only \(R\) avoids storing \(Q\), but this particular example retains the data window so that observations can be deleted and reference fits checked.

3 Least squares, ridge paths and model selection

The factors become statistically useful when they are connected to an estimation problem and to the predictions obtained from its solution. This chapter begins with ordinary least squares, where a coefficient vector can be checked against an independent QR fit, and then introduces ridge regularization. A ridge path shows how the estimates change with the penalty; cross-validation supplies a separate procedure for choosing among those candidate fits.

The construction of the design remains part of the model specification. These matrix interfaces do not insert an intercept or perform preprocessing automatically, so the examples make those choices explicit. Both ridge backends are checked against augmented-design QR calculations, allowing differences in model specification to be distinguished from differences between numerical implementations.

3.1 Least squares with predictions

Write the regression model as \(y=D\theta+\varepsilon\), where \(D=[\boldsymbol 1_n,X]\) includes an intercept and \(\theta=(\alpha,\beta^\top)^\top\). A direct thin factorization \(D=Q_D R_D\) gives the least-squares estimate through \(R_D\widehat\theta=Q_D^\top y\). The fitted values are \(D\widehat\theta\), while a new design with the same column definitions gives predictions \(D_{\mathrm{test}}\widehat\theta\).

The model-fitting interface used here, qrls(..., type = "QR"), solves a normalized cross-product system internally. The example therefore checks its coefficients against both a direct factorization of D and lm.fit(). On this well-conditioned design the three routes should agree to numerical precision; the accuracy chapter examines why their agreement on such an example does not establish identical numerical behavior near singularity.

We generate six predictors, of which three have nonzero coefficients, together with an intercept. Observation noise means that fitted coefficients need not equal their generating values exactly. The independent test observations are reserved for assessing prediction after the model has been fitted.

set.seed(2029)
n <- 160L
p <- 6L
n_test <- 400L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
X_test <- matrix(rnorm(n_test * p), n_test, p)
beta_true <- c(2, -1.5, .75, 0, 0, 0)
y <- drop(1 + X %*% beta_true + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5))
y_test <- drop(1 + X_test %*% beta_true + rnorm(n_test, sd = 1.5))
design <- cbind(intercept = 1, X)
design_test <- cbind(intercept = 1, X_test)
ols <- fastQR::qrls(y, design, X_test = design_test, type = "QR")
ols_factors <- fastQR::qr(design, complete = FALSE)
ols_projection <- crossprod(ols_factors$Q, y)
ols_explicit <- backsolve(ols_factors$R, ols_projection)
ols_derivation_error <- max(abs(ols$coeff - ols_explicit))
stopifnot(ols_derivation_error < 1e-10,
          max(abs(ols$coeff - lm.fit(design, y)$coefficients)) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  term = c("Intercept", paste0("x", seq_len(p))),
  truth = c(1, beta_true), estimate = as.numeric(ols$coeff)), digits = 4)
term truth estimate
Intercept 1.00 1.1081
x1 2.00 2.0667
x2 -1.50 -1.3108
x3 0.75 0.8603
x4 0.00 -0.0704
x5 0.00 -0.1605
x6 0.00 -0.0224 
ols_test_mse <- mean((y_test - drop(design_test %*% ols$coeff))^2)
ols_test_mse
## [1] 2.238406

The error on the independent test set estimates predictive performance; it is not the training residual variance. We compute the squared residual loss explicitly from predictions so that the quantity being reported is unambiguous.

Figure 2 compares the independent test responses with the predictions from the fitted model. The identity line represents exact prediction. Scatter around that line includes the new observation noise, so an accurate coefficient estimate does not make every test prediction coincide with its observed response.

ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(observed = y_test,
                          predicted = drop(design_test %*% ols$coeff)),
                ggplot2::aes(observed, predicted)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = .4, colour = "#b5121b") +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#526070") +
  ggplot2::coord_equal() + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

Figure 2: Independent test responses versus least-squares predictions. The diagonal is a reference line, not a fitted trend.

3.2 Ridge: scaling the penalty and handling the intercept

For either backend of qrridge(), the coefficient vector solves \[ \widehat\beta_\lambda =\arg\min_b\left\{\frac{1}{n}\|y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda\|b\|_2^2\right\} =(X^\top X+n\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^\top y. \] Differentiating this criterion with respect to b gives \[ -\frac{2}{n}X^\top(y-Xb)+2\lambda b=0, \] and hence the penalized system \((X^\top X+n\lambda I_p)\widehat\beta_\lambda=X^\top y\). A positive penalty adds curvature in every coefficient direction, making this system nonsingular even if the design has dependent columns. The inverse in the displayed expression describes the estimator mathematically; the implementations obtain it through factorizations and solves.

3.2.1 The two numerical routes

In the QR backend, define \(A_\lambda=X^\top X/n+\lambda I_p\) and \(h=X^\top y\). The routine factorizes \(A_\lambda=Q_A R_A\), forms \(Q_A^\top h/n\) and solves the upper triangular system with \(R_A\). The factorization is therefore of the normalized penalized system, rather than of X itself.

The R backend uses the augmented design \(\widetilde X=[X^\top,\sqrt{n\lambda}I_p]^\top\) to obtain a triangular factor \(\widetilde R\) satisfying \(\widetilde R^\top\widetilde R=X^\top X+n\lambda I_p\). The coefficients follow from \[ \widetilde R^\top c=h,\qquad \widetilde R\widehat\beta_\lambda=c. \] These routes have the same exact-arithmetic solution, while their intermediate factors have different meanings. The examples compare their coefficients with an independent augmented-design QR solve, rather than comparing their R entries as though they were the same factorization.

The factor n follows from normalizing the data loss by the number of observations. Replicating all observations leaves this criterion, and therefore the estimate at a fixed penalty, unchanged. In a validation fold the same convention uses the number of training observations, not the size of the full dataset.

3.2.2 Centering, scaling and coefficient interpretation

Here lambda is a scalar. We build a path by calling the function once per grid value. All supplied columns are penalized. To leave the intercept unpenalized, center the response and predictors, estimate the slopes, and reconstruct the intercept. We also scale predictors using training-set standard deviations so that a common penalty has a comparable interpretation across columns.

Let \(\bar x_j\) and \(s_j\) denote the training mean and standard deviation of predictor j, and define \(Z_{ij}=(X_{ij}-\bar x_j)/s_j\). Fitting the centered response on Z produces standardized coefficients \(\widehat\gamma_\lambda\). The original-scale slopes and intercept are recovered through \[ \widehat\beta_{\lambda,j}=\widehat\gamma_{\lambda,j}/s_j, \qquad \widehat\alpha_\lambda=\bar y-\sum_j\bar x_j\widehat\beta_{\lambda,j}. \] Thus a new prediction can be obtained either from the standardized design with the training means and scales, or from the original predictors with these recovered coefficients. The penalty acts on the standardized coefficients, which is why changing predictor units without an explicit scaling convention can change the fit.

x_mean <- colMeans(X)
x_scale <- apply(X, 2, sd)
y_mean <- mean(y)
Z <- sweep(sweep(X, 2, x_mean, "-"), 2, x_scale, "/")
y_centered <- y - y_mean
lambda <- exp(seq(log(1e-4), log(10), length.out = 50L))
path_standardized <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) {
  as.numeric(fastQR::qrridge(y_centered, Z, lambda = lam, type = "QR")$coeff)
}, numeric(p))
path_triangular <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) {
  as.numeric(fastQR::qrridge(y_centered, Z, lambda = lam, type = "R")$coeff)
}, numeric(p))
stopifnot(max(abs(path_standardized - path_triangular)) < 1e-10)
path_slopes <- sweep(path_standardized, 1, x_scale, "/")
path_intercept <- y_mean - drop(crossprod(x_mean, path_slopes))

# Independent augmented-design QR calculation at one grid value.
j <- 20L
reference <- qr.coef(base::qr(rbind(Z, sqrt(n * lambda[j]) * diag(p))),
                     c(y_centered, rep(0, p)))
stopifnot(max(abs(path_standardized[, j] - reference)) < 1e-10)

The R-only calculation at one path value can also be checked directly from its returned triangular factor. The inner forwardsolve() reconstructs the response coordinates, and the following backsolve() returns the coefficients. The additional rows in the augmented QR reference contain zeros in the response because they encode only the penalty.

ridge_R_fit <- fastQR::qrridge(y_centered, Z, lambda[j], type = "R")
ridge_rhs <- crossprod(Z, y_centered)
ridge_coordinates <- forwardsolve(t(ridge_R_fit$R), ridge_rhs)
ridge_explicit <- backsolve(ridge_R_fit$R, ridge_coordinates)
ridge_manual_error <- max(abs(ridge_explicit - path_triangular[, j]))
stopifnot(ridge_manual_error < 1e-10)

Figure 3 follows the fitted slopes as the penalty increases. Expressing the coefficients on the original predictor scale makes their statistical interpretation consistent with the data-generating model, while the logarithmic penalty axis reveals changes across several orders of magnitude. Agreement between the two numerical backends is checked before the paths are drawn.

path_table <- data.frame(lambda = rep(lambda, each = p),
                         coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), length(lambda))),
                         estimate = as.vector(path_slopes))
ggplot2::ggplot(path_table, ggplot2::aes(lambda, estimate, colour = coefficient)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) + ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Coefficient estimate", colour = "Predictor") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

Figure 3: Ridge slopes on their original predictor scale, plotted against a logarithmic penalty grid. The coefficients change continuously with the penalty; ridge does not generally create an exactly sparse fit.

3.3 Cross-validation with preprocessing inside each fold

A coefficient vector at a fixed penalty minimizes training loss plus a penalty term. Choosing the penalty is a separate calculation, for which the relevant target is prediction on observations not used to obtain those coefficients. Divide the training sample into validation sets \(\mathcal V_1,\ldots,\mathcal V_K\), and let \(\mathcal T_k\) contain the remaining observations for fold k. A candidate penalty is fitted on \(\mathcal T_k\) and evaluated on \(\mathcal V_k\).

The explicit loop below records a squared prediction error for every validation observation and averages those errors across the full sample, \[ \mathrm{CV}(\lambda) =\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in\mathcal V_k} \left(y_i-\widehat y_i^{(-k)}(\lambda)\right)^2. \] The same fold assignment is retained for every candidate penalty. Means, standard deviations and the response mean are estimated from \(\mathcal T_k\) alone, then applied to the held-out predictors. This reproduces the information available when predicting a genuinely new observation and prevents validation values from influencing the preprocessing used to fit that fold.

After selecting the smallest validation error, the final coefficient vector is taken from the path fitted on the full training sample. Its preprocessing uses the full training means and scales, as it should at this refitting stage. The independent test set remains outside both the fold calculations and the penalty selection.

set.seed(2030)
K <- 5L
fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = n))
squared_error <- matrix(NA_real_, n, length(lambda))
for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train <- fold != k
  valid <- !train
  mu <- colMeans(X[train, , drop = FALSE])
  sc <- apply(X[train, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
  ybar <- mean(y[train])
  Z_train <- sweep(sweep(X[train, , drop = FALSE], 2, mu, "-"), 2, sc, "/")
  Z_valid <- sweep(sweep(X[valid, , drop = FALSE], 2, mu, "-"), 2, sc, "/")
  for (j in seq_along(lambda)) {
    b <- fastQR::qrridge(y[train] - ybar, Z_train,
                         lambda = lambda[j], type = "QR")$coeff
    prediction <- ybar + drop(Z_valid %*% b)
    squared_error[valid, j] <- (y[valid] - prediction)^2
  }
}
cv_mse <- colMeans(squared_error)
best <- which.min(cv_mse)
lambda_selected <- lambda[best]
selected_prediction <- path_intercept[best] + drop(X_test %*% path_slopes[, best])
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  method = c("Least squares", "CV-selected ridge"),
  test_MSE = c(ols_test_mse, mean((y_test - selected_prediction)^2))), digits = 4)
method test_MSE
Least squares 2.2384
CV-selected ridge 2.2378 
lambda_selected
## [1] 0.001676833

The test responses are used only after selection. A single simulation need not favor ridge over least squares. Cross-validation chooses among the candidate penalties; it does not guarantee that the selected fit outperforms every alternative on new data. If the selected value lies at a grid endpoint, consider extending the grid.

The validation curve in Figure 4 summarizes the prediction loss over the candidate penalties. Its minimum identifies the value used for the final fit, with the dashed line locating that choice on the same grid. The curve concerns held-out prediction after fold-specific preprocessing; it is not the training loss minimized when estimating the coefficients.

ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(lambda, MSE = cv_mse), ggplot2::aes(lambda, MSE)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#b5121b", linewidth = .9) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = lambda_selected, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#526070") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Cross-validated MSE") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

Figure 4: Validation mean squared error along the penalty grid. The dashed line marks the minimum on this grid.

3.4 Effective degrees of freedom along the ridge path

For a fixed design, fixed preprocessing and fixed \(\lambda\), ridge is linear in \(y\). If \(d_j\) are the singular values of the centered, standardized design \(Z\), the effective degrees of freedom including the unpenalized intercept are \[ \mathrm{df}(\lambda)=1+\sum_{j=1}^p\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+n\lambda}. \] To see where this expression comes from, write the thin singular value decomposition \(Z=U_Z D_Z V_Z^\top\), with diagonal entries \(d_j\) in \(D_Z\). For the centered response \(y_c=y-\bar y\boldsymbol 1_n\), the centered fitted values are \[ \widehat y_c =H_\lambda y_c,\qquad H_\lambda =U_Z\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+n\lambda}\right)U_Z^\top. \] Each orthogonal data direction therefore contributes a shrinkage multiplier \(d_j^2/(d_j^2+n\lambda)\) to the fitted-value map. The trace of this matrix is the sum of those multipliers. Because Z has centered columns, the separate intercept adds the projection onto the constant direction and contributes one additional degree of freedom.

For a full-column-rank Z, the total approaches \(p+1\) as the penalty tends to zero and approaches one as it tends to infinity. These limits describe the unpenalized fit and the intercept-only limit. They do not require every coefficient on the original predictor scale to decrease monotonically when predictors are correlated.

The code computes this fixed-penalty trace explicitly, rather than reading the package’s legacy residual-dimension field df. Substituting a penalty selected from the responses locates a fit on the curve, but the trace of that candidate alone does not include the additional response dependence of the selection rule.

Figure 5 expresses the same regularization path in terms of effective model complexity. Increasing the penalty reduces the contribution of each penalized direction, while the unpenalized intercept contributes one degree of freedom throughout. The dashed line locates the selected penalty without incorporating the additional response dependence of the selection procedure into this fixed-penalty formula.

d2 <- svd(Z, nu = 0, nv = 0)$d^2
df_path <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) 1 + sum(d2 / (d2 + n * lam)), numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(diff(df_path) <= 0), all(df_path >= 1), all(df_path <= p + 1))
ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(lambda, df = df_path), ggplot2::aes(lambda, df)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#b5121b", linewidth = .9) + ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = lambda_selected, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Effective degrees of freedom") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

Figure 5: Effective degrees of freedom for each fixed ridge penalty, including the unpenalized intercept. The dashed line marks the cross-validated penalty; the curve describes fixed-penalty fits.

3.5 Multiple responses

With \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\), the model has a coefficient matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{p_D\times q}\), where \(p_D\) is the number of columns in the supplied design D. The least-squares loss is \(\|Y-DB\|_F^2\), the sum of the q response-specific squared losses. A direct factorization \(D=Q_D R_D\) yields \[ C=Q_D^\top Y,\qquad R_D\widehat B=C. \] The columns of C are projected response vectors. One triangular factor is reused to solve for all coefficient columns, so the common design does not need to be factorized separately for each outcome. The example checks qrmls() against both that direct calculation and a base-R QR fit.

set.seed(2031)
Y <- cbind(y, drop(-.5 + X %*% c(0, 1, 0, -1, 0, .5) + rnorm(n)))
multivariate <- fastQR::qrmls(Y, design, type = "QR")
reference <- qr.coef(base::qr(design), Y)
multi_direct <- backsolve(ols_factors$R, crossprod(ols_factors$Q, Y))
multi_direct_error <- max(abs(multivariate$coeff - multi_direct))
stopifnot(multi_direct_error < 1e-10,
          max(abs(multivariate$coeff - reference)) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(as.matrix(multivariate$coeff), digits = 4,
             col.names = c("Response 1", "Response 2"))
Response 1 Response 2
1.1081 -0.5143
2.0667 -0.0096
-1.3108 1.1742
0.8603 -0.0503
-0.0704 -0.9931
-0.1605 -0.0918
-0.0224 0.2954

3.6 Native cross-validation on a supplied design

The packaged interfaces select a penalty for the design matrix supplied to them. They do not center the response, standardize predictors within folds or treat a column of ones separately. Consequently, the following fit penalizes the intercept column in design. It answers a different model-selection question from the preceding example, where preprocessing is repeated within each fold and the intercept is unpenalized.

The native interfaces generate random folds from the supplied seed, and return their labels rather than accepting a user-supplied fold assignment. The independent simulated observations used here match that resampling setup. An explicit validation loop leaves the training and validation sets under the analyst’s control when a different prediction design is required, such as a chronological split of ordered observations.

Each training fit minimizes its own normalized loss, with the number of training observations multiplying the penalty in the normal equations. The returned foldid makes the split explicit. The reported curve averages held-out squared errors equally across folds; when fold sizes differ, this need not equal a pooled average across all validation observations.

native_qr <- fastQR::qrridge_cv(y, design, lambda, k = 5L, seed = 2032L,
                                X_test = design_test, type = "QR")
native_r <- fastQR::qrridge_cv(y, design, lambda, k = 5L, seed = 2032L,
                               X_test = design_test, type = "R")
stopifnot(identical(native_qr$foldid, native_r$foldid),
          max(abs(native_qr$mse - native_r$mse)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(native_qr$coeff - native_r$coeff)) < 1e-10)

# Reconstruct the entire validation curve independently.
native_reference_mse <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) {
  mean(vapply(sort(unique(native_qr$foldid)), function(k) {
    train <- native_qr$foldid != k
    valid <- !train
    nt <- sum(train)
    A <- rbind(design[train, , drop = FALSE],
               sqrt(nt * lam) * diag(ncol(design)))
    b <- qr.coef(base::qr(A), c(y[train], rep(0, ncol(design))))
    mean((y[valid] - drop(design[valid, , drop = FALSE] %*% b))^2)
  }, numeric(1)))
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(max(abs(as.numeric(native_qr$mse) - native_reference_mse)) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  backend = c("QR", "R"),
  selected_lambda = c(native_qr$lambda_min, native_r$lambda_min),
  validation_MSE = c(native_qr$mse_min, native_r$mse_min),
  test_MSE = c(mean((y_test - native_qr$predicted)^2),
               mean((y_test - native_r$predicted)^2))), digits = 5,
  caption = "Native cross-validation with a penalized intercept column.")
Native cross-validation with a penalized intercept column.
backend selected_lambda validation_MSE test_MSE
QR 0.02223 2.87428 2.22877
R 0.02223 2.87428 2.22877

The final coefficients are estimated again on the full training sample at the selected penalty. The mse_min_ind field retains a zero-based index for compatibility; lambda_min gives the selected value directly. For the R backend, an explicit orthogonal factor is neither needed nor returned.

3.7 Ridge with multiple responses

Ridge retains the shared-system structure for several outcomes. Differentiating \(\|Y-DB\|_F^2/n+\lambda\|B\|_F^2\) gives \[ (D^\top D+n\lambda I_{p_D})\widehat B_\lambda=D^\top Y. \] The right-hand side has q columns; each is processed using the same penalized factorization. The augmented reference stacks \(\sqrt{n\lambda}I_{p_D}\) below D and a \(p_D\times q\) zero matrix below Y, turning the penalized calculation into ordinary multivariate least squares.

The native validation score averages squared prediction errors over held-out rows and response columns within each fold, then averages the fold scores. Averaging over responses multiplies their summed prediction loss by the fixed factor \(1/q\), which does not change the ordering of candidate penalties for that response set. Different response units still change the relative contribution of the outcomes, so any desired response scaling must be specified explicitly and fitted within the training portions of the validation procedure.

multi_qr <- fastQR::qrmridge_cv(Y, design, lambda, k = 5L, seed = 2032L,
                                X_test = design_test, type = "QR")
multi_r <- fastQR::qrmridge_cv(Y, design, lambda, k = 5L, seed = 2032L,
                               X_test = design_test, type = "R")
A <- rbind(design, sqrt(n * multi_qr$lambda_min) * diag(ncol(design)))
B_reference <- qr.coef(base::qr(A), rbind(Y, matrix(0, ncol(design), ncol(Y))))
stopifnot(max(abs(multi_qr$coeff - B_reference)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(multi_r$coeff - B_reference)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(multi_qr$mse - multi_r$mse)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(multi_qr$predicted - design_test %*% B_reference)) < 1e-10,
          !anyDuplicated(names(multi_qr)), !anyDuplicated(names(multi_r)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  backend = c("QR", "R"),
  selected_lambda = c(multi_qr$lambda_min, multi_r$lambda_min),
  validation_MSE = c(multi_qr$mse_min, multi_r$mse_min),
  maximum_coefficient_error = c(max(abs(multi_qr$coeff - B_reference)),
                                max(abs(multi_r$coeff - B_reference)))),
  digits = 6, caption = "Multiple-response ridge checked against an independent QR fit.")
Multiple-response ridge checked against an independent QR fit.
backend selected_lambda validation_MSE maximum_coefficient_error
QR 0.028118 2.020752 0
R 0.028118 2.020752 0

The cross-products are available as XTX and XTY; XTy is retained as an alias of XTY. The returned df field is a legacy residual-dimension diagnostic, rather than the effective ridge degrees of freedom derived earlier. Likewise, residual variance and covariance estimates divided by n-p are diagnostics, not unbiased ridge variance estimators.

4 Choosing the ridge penalty by marginal likelihood

Cross-validation selects a penalty by measuring predictive performance on observations omitted from fitting. A probability model offers another route: the coefficient vector can be integrated out, leaving a marginal likelihood for the regularization parameter. This chapter develops that construction explicitly, including the normalization terms that would be lost by treating a penalized residual sum of squares as a likelihood on its own.

We first describe the Gaussian model and derive its marginal likelihood, then explain how the variance and penalty are estimated. The implementation uses a single singular value decomposition to avoid repeating a matrix factorization at every candidate penalty. An independent QR calculation verifies the resulting coefficients. The concluding simulations compare this empirical Bayes procedure with an efficient cross-validation calculation on both tall and wide designs, under a dense Gaussian signal and a sparse signal that departs from the assumed coefficient distribution.

Gaussian marginal likelihood and hyperparameter selection are treated in Rasmussen and Williams (2006), Chapters 2 and 5. For work specifically on fast marginal likelihood selection of ridge parameters using singular values, see Karabatsos (2015). The construction below fixes its own prior and profiles the noise variance; it should not be read as a reproduction of every prior or algorithm in those references.

4.1 A Gaussian model whose posterior mean is ridge

Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) be fixed, and suppose \[ y\mid\beta,\sigma^2\sim N_n(X\beta,\sigma^2I_n),\qquad \beta\mid\sigma^2,\lambda\sim N_p\!\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{n\lambda}I_p\right), \qquad \lambda>0. \] The prior has the same variance in every coefficient direction. Its meaning consequently depends on the units of the predictors: rescaling a column without transforming the prior changes the model. The examples use predictors generated on a common scale, with a known zero intercept. The package does not insert an intercept or standardize columns automatically.

Set \(\alpha=n\lambda\) and \(A_\alpha=X^\top X+\alpha I_p\). Multiplying the likelihood and prior gives a quadratic exponent proportional to \[ \|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\alpha\|\beta\|_2^2. \] Completing the square yields \[ \|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\alpha\|\beta\|_2^2 =q_\alpha+(\beta-\widehat\beta_\alpha)^\top A_\alpha (\beta-\widehat\beta_\alpha), \] where \[ \widehat\beta_\alpha=A_\alpha^{-1}X^\top y,\qquad q_\alpha=\|y-X\widehat\beta_\alpha\|_2^2+ \alpha\|\widehat\beta_\alpha\|_2^2. \] Thus the conditional posterior is \[ \beta\mid y,\sigma^2,\lambda\sim N_p(\widehat\beta_\alpha,\sigma^2 A_\alpha^{-1}). \] Its mean and mode coincide with the ridge coefficients for the normalized criterion used by qrridge(). The inverse notation specifies the mathematical result; the numerical calculations below use decompositions and solves.

4.2 Integrating the coefficients

Integration means evaluating the density of the observed response after averaging over the coefficient prior: \[ p(y\mid\sigma^2,\lambda)= \int_{\mathbb R^p}p(y\mid\beta,\sigma^2) p(\beta\mid\sigma^2,\lambda)\,\mathrm d\beta. \] Using the completed square, the Gaussian integral contributes \((2\pi\sigma^2)^{p/2}|A_\alpha|^{-1/2}\). Combining this factor with the likelihood and prior normalizations gives \[ p(y\mid\sigma^2,\lambda) =(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\alpha^{p/2}|A_\alpha|^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{q_\alpha}{2\sigma^2}\right). \] The determinant factor matters: it changes when the prior becomes more or less concentrated. Omitting it would not maximize this marginal likelihood.

The same result follows directly from adding independent Gaussian random vectors. Writing \[ C_\lambda=I_n+\frac{XX^\top}{n\lambda}, \] we obtain \[ y\mid\sigma^2,\lambda\sim N_n(0,\sigma^2 C_\lambda). \] The determinant identity and quadratic-form identity are \[ \log|C_\lambda|=\log|A_\alpha|-p\log\alpha, \qquad y^\top C_\lambda^{-1}y=q_\alpha. \] If \(R^\top R=A_\alpha\), the first quantity can also be evaluated as \[ \log|C_\lambda|=2\sum_{j=1}^p\log|R_{jj}|-p\log\alpha. \] This connects the criterion to the augmented QR factors used in the previous chapter. For the quadratic form, evaluating the penalized residual expression is preferable to subtracting the nearly equal quantities \(y^\top y\) and \(y^\top X\widehat\beta_\alpha\) when the fit is very close.

4.3 Profiling the variance and optimizing the penalty

For a given \(\lambda\), differentiation of the marginal log likelihood with respect to \(\sigma^2\) gives \[ \widehat\sigma^2_\lambda=\frac{q_\alpha}{n}. \] This is the maximum-likelihood estimate under the marginal model. It is not the residual diagnostic based on \(n-p\), nor a correction based on the smoother trace. Inserting it into the negative log likelihood leaves, up to a constant independent of \(\lambda\), \[ F(\lambda)=\frac12\left\{ n\log\!\left(\frac{q_\alpha}{n}\right)+\log|C_\lambda| \right\}. \] We minimize this one-dimensional function and then evaluate the ridge posterior mean at the selected penalty. The coefficients have been integrated out, while \(\sigma^2\) has been profiled and \(\lambda\) estimated. No prior on \(\lambda\) is integrated in this procedure, and no claim of fully Bayesian hyperparameter uncertainty is implied.

Optimization is performed on \(t=\log\lambda\), so every evaluated finite penalty is positive. A coarse grid locates candidate local minima; bounded searches refine their neighboring intervals, and the endpoints are compared explicitly. A finite grid cannot certify a global optimum for every possible response. A returned lower-bound solution calls for inspecting and, where appropriate, extending the search range rather than describing it as an interior optimum.

The implementation also evaluates the limiting model \(\lambda\to\infty\). In that limit the coefficient prior collapses at zero, \(C_\lambda\to I_n\), and the fitted mean is zero. A data set can support this limit. Reporting it explicitly avoids inventing a large but arbitrary finite optimum. At the other extreme, small penalties can produce weakly identified or boundary behavior, especially in saturated or nearly interpolating settings; positivity alone does not guarantee a well-separated interior maximum.

An unknown unpenalized intercept requires an additional treatment of the mean, for example through generalized least-squares profiling or a restricted-likelihood construction with its corresponding adjustment. Simply centering the response and retaining every term of the known-mean likelihood without justification would change the inferential argument. The present implementation uses the explicitly stated known-zero-mean model and does not implement REML.

4.3.1 The score equation and the conditional smoother trace

The singular values also give an interpretable derivative of the profile criterion. With \(t=\log\lambda\) and \(\alpha=n\exp(t)\), define \[ \dot q_\alpha=\sum_{j=1}^r z_j^2 \frac{\alpha d_j^2}{(d_j^2+\alpha)^2},\qquad d_\alpha=\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\alpha}. \] Differentiating the profile criterion gives \[ \frac{\mathrm d F}{\mathrm d t} =\frac12\left(\frac{n\dot q_\alpha}{q_\alpha}-d_\alpha\right). \] Here \(d_\alpha\) is the trace of the ridge smoother at a fixed penalty. An interior empirical Bayes optimum balances these two terms. This identity is useful for checking an optimizer, but it does not justify replacing the marginal-model variance estimate \(q_\alpha/n\) with a residual degrees-of-freedom adjustment. The numerical checks below compare the analytic derivative with a centered finite difference.

4.4 A single decomposition for the entire objective

Let \(X=UDV^\top\) be an economy singular value decomposition with \(r=\min(n,p)\) columns in \(U\), and write \(z=U^\top y\) and \(y_\perp=y-Uz\). Then \[ \log|C_\lambda|=\sum_{j=1}^r\log\!\left(1+\frac{d_j^2}{\alpha}\right), \qquad q_\alpha=\|y_\perp\|_2^2+ \sum_{j=1}^r z_j^2\frac{\alpha}{d_j^2+\alpha}. \] These formulas remain valid for zero singular values and for \(p>n\). Evaluating the residual component directly avoids obtaining its squared norm by subtraction. The logarithm is computed with log1p(), which preserves accuracy for small arguments. After preparation, evaluating a new penalty uses scalar operations on the stored singular values and projected response rather than a fresh decomposition.

The posterior mean is recovered as \[ \widehat\beta_\alpha=V\,\operatorname{diag} \!\left(\frac{d_j}{d_j^2+\alpha}\right)z. \] This is a computational alternative to repeatedly refactorizing the augmented design. The SVD is included in the measured cost of penalty selection below; it is not treated as an available free input.

evidence_X <- evidence_results$demo$X
evidence_y <- evidence_results$demo$y
evidence_fit <- evidence_results$demo$fit
knitr::kable(data.frame(lambda = evidence_fit$lambda,
                        alpha = evidence_fit$alpha,
                        sigma2 = evidence_fit$sigma2,
                        status = evidence_fit$status), digits = 5,
             caption = "Empirical Bayes penalty and marginal-model variance estimate for the reproducible example.")

The estimated penalty can be passed directly to the package’s normalized ridge interface when it is finite. The following comparison checks that the posterior mean computed from singular values agrees with the augmented-factor implementation.

if (is.finite(evidence_fit$lambda)) {
  evidence_native <- fastQR::qrridge(evidence_y, evidence_X,
                                    evidence_fit$lambda, type = "R")
  evidence_native_error <- max(abs(evidence_native$coeff - evidence_fit$coeff))
  stopifnot(evidence_native_error < 1e-10)
  evidence_native_error
}

The criterion is verified against a direct Cholesky factorization of the response covariance \(C_\lambda\) at several positive penalties. The coefficient calculation is checked against QR of the augmented design with an orthogonally transformed response. A further identity check compares \(q_\alpha\) with the sum of squared residuals and the coefficient penalty. These calculations use different numerical representations of the same model.

evidence_check_table[, -1] <- lapply(evidence_check_table[, -1],
  function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 2))

4.6 Comparing marginal likelihood and cross-validation

Both selectors operate on the same training samples and use the same predictor units. The simulation considers \((n,p)=(100,40)\) and \((60,100)\), with independent standard-normal predictors and unit noise variance. In the dense scenario, coefficients are generated independently from \(N(0,4/p)\), which matches the spherical prior structure. In the sparse scenario, three coefficients equal two and the remaining coefficients are zero. The latter intentionally departs from that prior. Five independently seeded training samples are generated for each setting, and each sample has an independent test set of four hundred observations.

For cross-validation, five training folds each receive their own SVD, reused over a common grid of thirty-one penalties from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^2\). The training criterion uses the actual training size \(n_{\rm train}\lambda\), and the validation errors are averaged across folds. After selection, a full-data decomposition provides the coefficients. The spectral CV calculation is checked against qrridge_cv() using the same fold assignment; its maximum discrepancy is 5.11e-15.

This efficient CV baseline avoids attributing an advantage to marginal likelihood merely because the competing implementation repeats a decomposition at every penalty. Both timing measurements include selection and the final coefficient calculation, with warm-up and three calibrated repetitions. Test-data generation and evaluation are outside the timed regions. The empirical Bayes search is continuous within refined log-penalty intervals, whereas CV selects from a specified finite grid; the two methods also target different statistical criteria.

Both costs include the required decompositions and recovery of the selected coefficients. This timing result compares two different selection criteria; it is not evidence that the empirical Bayes selector has uniformly lower predictive error. 4.7 What changes when data or predictors are updated?

The preceding chapter holds a specified penalty fixed while updating a factor. Selecting the penalty again is additional work. A factor for \(X^\top X+\alpha_0I_p\) is not also a factor for \(X^\top X+\alpha I_p\) when \(\alpha\ne\alpha_0\). An update advantage at a fixed penalty consequently cannot be transferred directly to the complete reselected estimator. This chapter uses a reusable spectral representation for the penalty search and the QR-based package interface to verify the selected fit.

Likewise, conditional posterior covariance at estimated hyperparameters omits uncertainty about those hyperparameters. A fully Bayesian analysis would specify and average over their posterior distribution. The fixed-penalty smoother trace also remains a conditional complexity measure: after the penalty is selected from the response, it is not automatically the divergence or degrees of freedom of the complete selected fitting rule. These distinctions keep computational reuse, penalty estimation and uncertainty assessment separate and explicit.

5 Ridge regression as the design grows

A sequence of ridge fits provides a useful setting in which to assess the value of updating a triangular factor. New observations change the information available about a fixed coefficient vector, whereas new predictors enlarge the model itself. Both operations can be represented as changes to an augmented least-squares design. This representation also allows us to consider more predictors than observations: a positive ridge penalty makes the augmented design full column rank even when the observed design is wide.

The comparison in this chapter concerns the numerical work required to fit the same specified model after a change in its design. We examine coefficient and prediction accuracy separately from elapsed time, and compare updating with a fresh LAPACK factorization of the augmented design. The penalty is specified in advance. Choosing it from the data is a separate procedure, discussed in the preceding chapter.

5.1 The augmented problem and the meaning of a fixed penalty

For a response matrix \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\) and design \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), consider \[ \widehat B_\alpha=\arg\min_B\{\|Y-XB\|_F^2+\alpha\|B\|_F^2\},\qquad \alpha>0. \] Writing \[ A_\alpha=\begin{bmatrix}X\\\sqrt\alpha I_p\end{bmatrix},\qquad Y_\alpha=\begin{bmatrix}Y\\0_{p\times q}\end{bmatrix} \] turns this criterion into an ordinary least-squares problem with a full-column-rank design. Indeed, for any nonzero vector \(v\), \[ v^\top A_\alpha^\top A_\alpha v=\|Xv\|_2^2+\alpha\|v\|_2^2>0. \] This argument does not require \(p\le n\). If \(A_\alpha=QR\), then \[ R^\top R=X^\top X+\alpha I_p,\qquad R^\top Z=X^\top Y,\qquad R\widehat B_\alpha=Z. \] The last two equations describe an R-only workflow, which maintains the response cross-product as well as the factor. They are not interchangeable, in numerical accuracy, with explicitly applying the orthogonal transformations to \(Y_\alpha\). We therefore use the latter approach as an independent reference when checking the updated coefficients. The use of QR and augmented systems for least squares is discussed in Golub and Van Loan (2013) and Björck (2015).

The public ridge functions use the normalized criterion \(\|Y-XB\|_F^2/n+\lambda\|B\|_F^2\), so the parameter in the augmented design is \(\alpha=n\lambda\). Holding \(\alpha\) fixed while adding observations consequently changes the equivalent normalized parameter to \(\lambda_{n+m}=\alpha/(n+m)\). Holding \(\lambda\) fixed instead changes the total penalty. We treat these two experiments separately rather than silently changing the optimization problem.

5.2 A reproducible fit with more predictors than observations

The following example has forty observations and eighty predictors. A positive penalty gives a unique fit, despite the rank deficiency of the unpenalized problem. The two public interfaces are compared with a QR solve of the augmented design, whose right-hand side is transformed orthogonally.

set.seed(312)
n_wide <- 40L
p_wide <- 80L
X_wide <- matrix(rnorm(n_wide * p_wide), n_wide, p_wide)
y_wide <- rnorm(n_wide)
alpha_wide <- 8
lambda_wide <- alpha_wide / n_wide
wide_QR <- fastQR::qrridge(y_wide, X_wide, lambda_wide, type = "QR")
wide_R <- fastQR::qrridge(y_wide, X_wide, lambda_wide, type = "R")
A_wide <- rbind(X_wide, sqrt(alpha_wide) * diag(p_wide))
f_wide <- fastQR::qr_lapack(A_wide, output = "thin")
beta_reference <- backsolve(
  f_wide$R, crossprod(f_wide$Q, c(y_wide, rep(0, p_wide))))
c(QR_error = max(abs(wide_QR$coeff - beta_reference)),
  R_error = max(abs(wide_R$coeff - beta_reference)))
##     QR_error      R_error 
## 1.137979e-15 5.273559e-16
stopifnot(max(abs(wide_QR$coeff - beta_reference)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(wide_R$coeff - beta_reference)) < 1e-10)

The legacy residual diagnostic \(n-p\) is not a degrees-of-freedom formula for ridge regression. The updated interfaces return NA for this diagnostic and its associated variance estimates when \(p>n\); the coefficients, fitted values and requested predictions remain available. Effective ridge degrees of freedom are obtained from the smoother matrix, as explained in the preceding chapter. A zero penalty still requires full column rank, and therefore cannot be used to obtain a unique wide-design fit through these interfaces.

5.3 Adding observations

Suppose that \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}\) contains new observations and \(V\in\mathbb R^{m\times q}\) their responses. At fixed \(\alpha\), the maintained quantities satisfy \[ R_{\rm new}^\top R_{\rm new}=R^\top R+U^\top U, \qquad H_{\rm new}=H+U^\top V,\qquad H=X^\top Y. \] The existing row-update routine applies to the augmented design. The penalty rows need not be added again: they are already represented in \(R\).

set.seed(313)
new_X <- matrix(rnorm(5L * p_wide), 5L, p_wide)
new_y <- rnorm(5L)
R_before <- fastQR::qr_lapack(A_wide, output = "R")
H_before <- crossprod(X_wide, y_wide)
R_after <- fastQR::rupdate(A_wide, R_before, U = t(new_X),
                          type = "row", fast = FALSE)
H_after <- H_before + crossprod(new_X, new_y)
beta_after <- backsolve(R_after, forwardsolve(t(R_after), H_after))
fit_after <- fastQR::qrridge(c(y_wide, new_y), rbind(X_wide, new_X),
                            lambda = alpha_wide / (n_wide + 5L), type = "R")
stopifnot(max(abs(beta_after - fit_after$coeff)) < 1e-10)

If the normalized parameter \(\lambda\) must remain fixed, the required identity is instead \[ R_{\rm new}^\top R_{\rm new} =R^\top R+U^\top U+m\lambda I_p. \] One valid construction appends both the observation rows and the additional penalty rows \(\sqrt{m\lambda}I_p\). This construction is exact, but its extra work can erase an advantage for updating. The timing comparison below includes this cost; a fixed-\(\alpha\) result must not be presented as evidence of a fixed-\(\lambda\) speedup.

5.4 Adding predictors

Let \(W\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) contain new predictors. With the same penalty on every coefficient, the enlarged augmented design can be arranged as \[ \begin{bmatrix} X&W\\\sqrt\alpha I_p&0\\0&\sqrt\alpha I_k \end{bmatrix}. \] The first \(p\) columns are the old augmented design with \(k\) zero rows appended. Their triangular factor is still \(R\). The new columns have observation part \(W\), zeros on the old penalty rows, and their own diagonal penalty block. Updating these columns therefore includes the penalty on the new coefficients; appending \(W\) alone would solve a different problem.

set.seed(314)
k_new <- 3L
W_new <- matrix(rnorm(n_wide * k_new), n_wide, k_new)
A_padded <- rbind(A_wide, matrix(0, k_new, p_wide))
W_augmented <- rbind(W_new, matrix(0, p_wide, k_new),
                     sqrt(alpha_wide) * diag(k_new))
R_enlarged <- fastQR::rupdate(A_padded, R_before, U = W_augmented,
                             type = "column", fast = FALSE)
H_enlarged <- rbind(H_before, crossprod(W_new, y_wide))
beta_enlarged <- backsolve(R_enlarged,
                           forwardsolve(t(R_enlarged), H_enlarged))
fit_enlarged <- fastQR::qrridge(y_wide, cbind(X_wide, W_new),
                               lambda_wide, type = "R")
stopifnot(max(abs(beta_enlarged - fit_enlarged$coeff)) < 1e-10)

This column update includes a triangular solve whose accuracy depends on conditioning. The positive penalty separates the augmented columns from exact linear dependence, but does not provide a uniform accuracy guarantee for arbitrarily small penalties. The tests below use a moderate specified penalty and report the observed errors against an orthogonal reference.

5.5 Accuracy and time for the same updated fit

The experiments use tall and wide observed designs, two response variables, batches of ten observations or five predictors, and five calibrated timed repetitions after warm-up. Both timed workflows return coefficients through an R-only solve. The update starts from existing factors and a cached response cross-product; the alternative rebuilds the augmented factor and response cross-product. Construction of the augmented matrices needed by each workflow and the final triangular solves are included. Random-data generation, validation and initial factorization are excluded from these single-change measurements. The reference uses LAPACK without pivoting in both cases.

The difference between the two row experiments is part of the computational question. An observation update at fixed total penalty modifies only the data contribution, whereas retaining a fixed normalized penalty also modifies the regularization block. Likewise, a predictor update must introduce the new penalty directions. The measured comparison, including these operations, determines whether maintaining the factor is advantageous on a particular problem. The complete repetitions and validation values are saved with the guide rather than replaced by a universal speed claim.

5.6 Following the design across the boundary \(p=n\)

A sequence of changes tests whether errors accumulate in ways that a single update can conceal. One experiment adds predictors to a design with one hundred observations, increasing its width from sixty to one hundred and sixty columns. A second adds observations to a design with one hundred predictors, increasing its sample size from sixty to one hundred and sixty. Both hold \(\alpha=20\) fixed and cross the unpenalized boundary \(p=n\), while their augmented designs remain full column rank throughout.

Figure 8 displays the cumulative numerical work along each sequence. The same initial factorization cost is included in both curves. These path measurements are single elapsed-time trajectories, whereas the preceding table uses repeated calibrated calls. Small elapsed-time differences along the paths should therefore be read cautiously.

The paths show how the factor and response information can be reused through a changing statistical model. They do not include selecting the penalty, and their times do not include evaluating predictions over a separate large test set. The distinction between maintaining numerical information and choosing a model is essential when using these examples to motivate a statistical application.

6 Numerical accuracy and reproducible timing

A numerical method has to produce an adequate answer before its execution time becomes informative. For matrix factorizations, this involves checking both the identities satisfied by the returned factors and the accuracy of the calculations that use them. These checks address different parts of a statistical computation: reconstructing a design accurately does not, by itself, establish that its regression coefficients can be estimated accurately when the design is nearly singular.

The timing experiments therefore follow the numerical comparisons. Each experiment specifies the information available at its starting point and the representation required at its end. Compact Householder information, explicit thin factors and complete factors involve different amounts of computation and storage. Keeping those requests separate makes the measurements relevant to an actual choice of workflow.

6.1 Accuracy as the condition number increases

The purpose of this experiment is to separate the quality of a factorization from the sensitivity of a coefficient estimate. Random Gaussian designs of a fixed shape are often reasonably well conditioned, so they do not provide a controlled way to study what happens near a rank deficiency. Instead, we construct each design from prescribed singular values, \[ X=U\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_p)V^\top, \qquad U^\top U=I_p,\qquad V^\top V=I_p. \] Here U has n rows and p orthonormal columns, while V is a square p-dimensional orthogonal matrix. The code obtains them by factorizing random matrices with base R and extracting their orthogonal factors.

The largest singular value is fixed at one, while the smallest is set to \(1/\kappa_\star\). The intermediate values are spaced geometrically. The resulting spectral condition number is therefore \(\kappa_2(X)=\kappa_\star\), up to floating-point rounding. Holding the orthogonal matrices \(U\) and \(V\) fixed across the sequence changes the separation of the singular values without introducing a new random orientation at every step.

A small singular value identifies a direction in coefficient space whose effect on the response is small. Recovering that component of a coefficient vector requires amplifying the corresponding response component, making the solution sensitive to small perturbations. To examine this numerical effect without additional observation noise, we choose a known coefficient vector \(\beta\) and form \(y=X\beta\). The reference coefficients are then available directly, rather than being supplied by another numerical solver.

We record two relative errors, \[ E_{\mathrm{rec}} =\frac{\|X-\widehat Q\widehat R\|_F}{\|X\|_F}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{coef}} =\frac{\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_2}{\|\beta\|_2}. \] The first measures how closely the factors represent the input matrix. The second measures the error in the coefficients obtained after applying those factors to the response and solving the triangular system. An accurate representation of \(X\) can coexist with a larger coefficient error because the inverse problem becomes more sensitive as \(\kappa_2(X)\) grows. The experiment includes a normal-equation solve to show the additional effect of explicitly forming \(X^\top X\) (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2015).

6.1.1 Computing the two coefficient estimates

For each design, fastQR::qr(X, complete = FALSE) returns \(Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) and \(R_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\). The direct QR estimate is obtained from \[ c=Q_1^\top y,\qquad R_1\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{QR}}=c. \] The first operation expresses the response in the orthonormal basis. The second recovers its coefficients relative to the original design columns. The projection identity \[ \|y-Xb\|_2^2 =\|Q_1^\top y-R_1b\|_2^2+\|(I_n-Q_1Q_1^\top)y\|_2^2 \] shows why this solves the least-squares problem: the final term is independent of b, and the triangular solve makes the first term zero. In the code, crossprod(f$Q, y) computes c and backsolve(f$R, c) performs the backward substitution. The factor R has the same singular values as X, so this solve remains sensitive when the design is ill conditioned; using QR does not make that sensitivity disappear.

The normal-equation estimate is computed through a different numerical route, \[ A=X^\top X,\qquad h=X^\top y,\qquad A\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{NE}}=h. \] These equations define the same coefficient vector in exact arithmetic when X has full column rank. They are represented by solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)) in the experiment. Forming A explicitly introduces rounding into a system whose condition number is the square of that of X. The comparison therefore separates the sensitivity of the original coefficient problem from the additional effects of the computational route used to solve it.

set.seed(2032)
n <- 160L
p <- 12L
U <- qr.Q(base::qr(matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)))
V <- qr.Q(base::qr(matrix(rnorm(p * p), p, p)))
beta <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = p)
condition_numbers <- 10^(0:8)
accuracy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(condition_numbers, function(kappa_target) {
  singular_values <- exp(seq(0, -log(kappa_target), length.out = p))
  X <- sweep(U, 2, singular_values, "*") %*% t(V)
  y <- drop(X %*% beta)
  f <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = FALSE)
  projected_response <- crossprod(f$Q, y)  # p coordinates in the Q basis
  b_qr <- backsolve(f$R, projected_response) # solve R beta = Q' y
  b_normal <- tryCatch(solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)),
                        error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, p))
  data.frame(condition = kappa_target,
    reconstruction = norm(X - f$Q %*% f$R, "F") / norm(X, "F"),
    QR_coefficients = sqrt(sum((b_qr - beta)^2) / sum(beta^2)),
    normal_equations = sqrt(sum((b_normal - beta)^2) / sum(beta^2)))
}))
knitr::kable(accuracy, digits = 12)

1e+02 0 0.000e+00 0.000000e+00
