1e+04 0 0.000e+00 4.211000e-09
1e+05 0 0.000e+00 3.986400e-08
1e+06 0 6.000e-12 1.390555e-05
1e+07 0 2.800e-11 2.664383e-03
1e+08 0 1.338e-09 NA 
stopifnot(max(accuracy$reconstruction) < 1e-10)

Figure 10 places the reconstruction and coefficient errors on logarithmic axes so that their different dependence on conditioning can be examined together. A flat reconstruction curve alongside a rising coefficient-error curve is compatible with an accurate factorization of a sensitive problem.

accuracy_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(condition = accuracy$condition, error = accuracy$reconstruction, metric = "QR reconstruction"),
  data.frame(condition = accuracy$condition, error = accuracy$QR_coefficients, metric = "QR coefficient solve"),
  data.frame(condition = accuracy$condition, error = accuracy$normal_equations, metric = "Normal-equation solve"))
ggplot2::ggplot(accuracy_long, ggplot2::aes(condition, pmax(error, .Machine$double.eps), colour = metric)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(na.rm = TRUE) + ggplot2::geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(kappa[2](X)), y = "Relative error", colour = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Figure 10: Relative reconstruction and coefficient errors versus the prescribed condition number. Missing normal-equation values indicate that the reference solver rejected the system as numerically singular.

For a full-column-rank design, \(\kappa_2(X^\top X)=\kappa_2(X)^2\). Thus a design with condition number \(10^8\) produces a cross-product matrix with condition number approximately \(10^{16}\), close to the reciprocal of double-precision machine accuracy. Rounding in the formation of the cross-products can then have a substantial effect, and a solver may reasonably treat the resulting system as numerically singular. Missing points on the normal-equation curve indicate such a rejection; they do not represent zero error.

The QR coefficient curve comes from the explicit projection and triangular solve displayed in the code. Its comparison with the reconstruction curve concerns these particular calculations, rather than every possible use of a QR representation. Values smaller than machine epsilon are placed at epsilon in the plot to keep the logarithmic display readable; the underlying numerical values remain in the table.

6.2 Timing a row update against refactorization

The computational advantage of updating is relevant when a factorization is already available and only a small part of the design changes. The next experiment represents that situation by starting with a factor of an existing design and appending ten observations. Each method is asked to process the same enlarged matrix, but the methods differ in the information they produce.

The R-only update modifies the available triangular factor. A fresh rchol() call reconstructs a triangular factor from the enlarged design, providing a comparison with the same returned representation. A fresh thin QR calculation also constructs an explicit orthogonal factor. Its time is useful when that larger output is needed, while its difference from the R-only update includes both the cost of refactorization and the cost of returning Q. The initial factorization is excluded from the update timing because it is assumed to have been performed before the new observations arrive.

We use three design sizes, ten new rows, five repetitions, warm-up calls and adaptively sized batches to reduce clock-resolution effects. Random-data generation, correctness checks and plotting are excluded from timed regions. The reported times are seconds per call, not elapsed time for an entire batch.

set.seed(2033)
repetitions <- 5L
sizes <- c(500L, 1000L, 2000L)
p <- 40L
m <- 10L
elapsed_per_call <- function(fun, batch_size) {
  unname(system.time(for (i in seq_len(batch_size)) fun())["elapsed"]) / batch_size
}
timing <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  U <- matrix(rnorm(p * m), p, m)
  X_new <- rbind(X, t(U))
  R <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = FALSE)$R
  methods <- list(
    "R update" = function() fastQR::rupdate(X, R, U, type = "row", fast = FALSE),
    "Fresh thin QR" = function() fastQR::qr(X_new, complete = FALSE),
    "Fresh R only" = function() fastQR::rchol(X_new))
  updated <- methods[[1]]()
  gram_error <- norm(crossprod(updated) - crossprod(X_new), "F") / norm(crossprod(X_new), "F")
  stopifnot(gram_error < 1e-10)
  invisible(lapply(methods, function(fun) fun()))
  batches <- vapply(methods, function(fun) {
    b <- 1L
    repeat {
      elapsed <- unname(system.time(for (i in seq_len(b)) fun())["elapsed"])
      if (elapsed >= .05 || b >= 4096L) break
      b <- b * 2L
    }
    b
  }, integer(1))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(repetitions), function(rep) {
    # Randomize execution order within each repetition.
    order <- sample(names(methods))
    data.frame(n = n, p = p, added_rows = m, repetition = rep, method = order,
      batch_calls = unname(batches[order]),
      seconds = vapply(order, function(name)
        elapsed_per_call(methods[[name]], batches[[name]]), numeric(1)))
  }))
}))
timing_summary <- aggregate(seconds ~ n + method, timing, median)
knitr::kable(timing_summary, digits = 6,
             col.names = c("Original rows", "Method", "Median seconds per call"))
Original rows Method Median seconds per call
500 Fresh R only 0.000293
1000 Fresh R only 0.000586
2000 Fresh R only 0.001187
500 Fresh thin QR 0.000797
1000 Fresh thin QR 0.001656
2000 Fresh thin QR 0.003250
500 R update 0.000022
1000 R update 0.000029
2000 R update 0.000043

Figure 11 compares the observed timings across the three row counts. The R-only update and R-only refactorization return the same kind of triangular factor. The fresh thin-QR calculation also constructs an explicit orthogonal factor, so its additional cost must be interpreted together with that larger output request.

ggplot2::ggplot(timing, ggplot2::aes(factor(n), seconds * 1000, colour = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .8), outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .8), size = 1.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Original number of observations", y = "Milliseconds per call (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Figure 11: Measured time to obtain factors after adding ten observations. Initial factors are assumed available for the update. Points and boxes summarize five repetitions; each repetition averages a calibrated batch of calls. Each design has 40 columns and receives 10 new rows.

At the largest row count in this run, updating the available factor takes a median of 0.043 milliseconds, compared with 1.19 milliseconds for R-only refactorization. This comparison applies to ten added rows and excludes the initial factorization from the update cost. The fresh thin-QR method also constructs \(Q\), so it answers a more demanding output request.

Timings depend on the machine, BLAS implementation, thread configuration and workload. A value printed as zero is below timer resolution and should not be interpreted as zero computational cost; increase the calibration duration if this occurs. These results illustrate this workload and do not establish a universal speed ranking. The code deliberately keeps input checking enabled.

6.3 Comparing QR interfaces

A compact factorization and an explicit basis can be used to solve the same mathematical problem while returning different amounts of information. A compact QR call stores R together with vectors and coefficients that describe Q. It can later apply those transformations to a response without forming Q. An explicit thin factorization has already performed that additional construction, while a pivoted factorization has also selected and recorded a column ordering.

Consequently, the interface-level table below identifies the exact call being timed. It describes the cost paid at that point in a workflow, rather than treating every object named QR as an identical output. The matched LAPACK experiment later in this chapter separately asks for the same thin or triangular representation from each implementation.

This comparison retains the five interfaces of the original benchmark: base::qr, fastQR::qr, fastQR::qr_fast with and without pivoting, and Matrix::qr. These calls return different representations: the timings compare the named interfaces, not identical output objects. The Matrix call below receives an ordinary dense R matrix, as in the original example; it is not a sparse-QR benchmark. Pivoting also performs additional work.

The default settings keep rebuilding this guide practical. Set options(fastQR.guide.full_benchmarks = TRUE) before source("build.R") to use the original large dimension grid and twenty repetitions in the scaling experiments. All displayed tables are generated from the actual settings, without loading historical timing files.

full_benchmarks <- isTRUE(getOption("fastQR.guide.full_benchmarks", FALSE))
benchmark_reps <- if (full_benchmarks) 20L else 5L
benchmark_n <- if (full_benchmarks) 2000L else 500L
benchmark_p <- if (full_benchmarks) c(20L,40L,100L,200L,400L,800L,1200L,1500L,1800L) else c(20L,40L,80L)
measure_methods <- function(methods, repetitions) {
  invisible(lapply(methods, function(f) f()))
  batches <- vapply(methods, function(f) {
    b <- 1L
    repeat {
      seconds <- unname(system.time(for (i in seq_len(b)) f())["elapsed"])
      if (seconds >= .05 || b >= 4096L) break
      b <- b * 2L
    }
    b
  }, integer(1))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(repetitions), function(rep) {
    order <- sample(names(methods))
    data.frame(repetition = rep, method = order, batch_calls = unname(batches[order]),
      seconds = vapply(order, function(k) elapsed_per_call(methods[[k]], batches[[k]]), numeric(1)))
  }))
}
set.seed(2041)
interface_n <- if (full_benchmarks) 1000L else 300L
interface_p <- if (full_benchmarks) 500L else 60L
interface_reps <- if (full_benchmarks) 10L else 5L
X_interface <- matrix(rnorm(interface_n * interface_p, 1), interface_n, interface_p)
interface_methods <- list(
  "base::qr (compact)" = function() base::qr(X_interface),
  "fastQR::qr (thin)" = function() fastQR::qr(X_interface, nb = 5, complete = FALSE),
  "qr_fast, no pivot" = function() fastQR::qr_fast(X_interface, pivot = FALSE),
  "qr_fast, pivot" = function() fastQR::qr_fast(X_interface, pivot = TRUE),
  "Matrix::qr (dense input)" = function() Matrix::qr(X_interface))
interface_timing <- measure_methods(interface_methods, interface_reps)
knitr::kable(aggregate(seconds ~ method, interface_timing, median), digits = 6,
  caption = sprintf("Median seconds per call: n = %d, p = %d, repetitions = %d.",
                    interface_n, interface_p, interface_reps))
Median seconds per call: n = 300, p = 60, repetitions = 5.
method seconds
Matrix::qr (dense input) 0.000195
base::qr (compact) 0.000199
fastQR::qr (thin) 0.000379
qr_fast, no pivot 0.000189
qr_fast, pivot 0.000166

In this run, the smallest median time in the interface table belongs to qr_fast, pivot. This is a comparison of calls with different outputs: forming explicit thin factors includes work that a compact representation defers. Pivoting can change the algorithm and its cost; a small observed timing difference is not evidence that pivoting is intrinsically free or beneficial.

6.4 QR, Cholesky and linear-system scaling benchmarks

These experiments vary the number of predictors while keeping the observation count fixed. The QR workload compares factorization interfaces. The triangular-factor workload distinguishes starting from X from starting with \(X^\top X\) already available. The solution workload starts even further downstream, with a common system \(A\beta=h\) supplied to each solver.

That starting point matters for interpretation. If \(A=X^\top X\) and \(h=X^\top y\), factorizing A by QR still solves the normal equations: it does not undo the earlier formation of the cross-products. A direct QR least-squares calculation instead factorizes X and applies its transformations to y. Both routes can agree closely on a well-conditioned example, while their behavior can differ as conditioning deteriorates.

We retain both block-size choices, \(5\) and \(p/2\), and the three workloads from the original vignette. Within each dimension, every method receives the same data. Input generation, validation and plotting are excluded from the timings; execution order is randomized within each repetition, and calls are batched to reduce clock-resolution effects. Repetitions measure timing variability on a fixed matrix, rather than variation across independently generated problems.

  • QR decomposition: fastQR::qr returns explicit thin factors, whereas base::qr returns compact factors. The different outputs must be considered when interpreting execution times.
  • Triangular factor: qrchol(X) is compared with both chol(crossprod(X)), which includes forming the Gram matrix, and chol(G) with \(G=X^\top X\) already available. Keeping both baselines makes the cost of forming \(G\) explicit.
  • Linear-system solution: both solvers receive the same precomputed \(G=X^\top X\) and \(h=X^\top y\). Thus neither method is charged for forming these inputs. This reproduces the original normal-equation workload; it is not a comparison of direct least-squares solvers acting on \(X\).
set.seed(2042)
benchmark_validation <- list()
scaling_timing <- do.call(rbind, lapply(benchmark_p, function(p) {
  n <- benchmark_n
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  y <- rnorm(n)
  G <- crossprod(X); h <- crossprod(X, y)
  block <- max(1L, p %/% 2L)
  b_reference <- base::qr.solve(G, h)
  errors <- numeric()
  for (nb in c(5L, block)) {
    f <- fastQR::qr(X, nb = nb, complete = FALSE)
    U <- fastQR::qrchol(X, nb = nb)
    b <- fastQR::qrsolve(A = G, b = h, nb = nb)
    errors <- c(errors, norm(X - f$Q %*% f$R, "F") / norm(X, "F"),
      norm(crossprod(U) - G, "F") / norm(G, "F"),
      sqrt(sum((b - b_reference)^2)) / max(1, sqrt(sum(b_reference^2))))
  }
  stopifnot(max(errors) < 1e-8)
  benchmark_validation[[as.character(p)]] <<- data.frame(p = p, max_relative_error = max(errors))
  workloads <- list(
    QR = list("fastQR, nb = 5" = function() fastQR::qr(X, nb = 5, complete = FALSE),
      "fastQR, nb = p/2" = function() fastQR::qr(X, nb = block, complete = FALSE),
      "base QR (compact)" = function() base::qr(X)),
    Cholesky = list("qrchol, nb = 5" = function() fastQR::qrchol(X, nb = 5),
      "qrchol, nb = p/2" = function() fastQR::qrchol(X, nb = block),
      "chol, Gram available" = function() base::chol(G),
      "crossprod + chol" = function() base::chol(crossprod(X))),
    Solve = list("qrsolve, nb = 5" = function() fastQR::qrsolve(G, h, nb = 5),
      "qrsolve, nb = p/2" = function() fastQR::qrsolve(G, h, nb = block),
      "base qr.solve" = function() base::qr.solve(G, h)))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(workloads), function(workload) {
    out <- measure_methods(workloads[[workload]], benchmark_reps)
    out$workload <- workload; out$n <- n; out$p <- p
    out
  }))
}))
benchmark_validation <- do.call(rbind, benchmark_validation)
knitr::kable(benchmark_validation, digits = 12,
             caption = "Largest relative validation error across the two block sizes and three workloads.")

benchmark_plot <- function(workload_name) {
  dat <- subset(scaling_timing, workload == workload_name)
  ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(factor(p), seconds * 1000, colour = method)) +
    ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, position = ggplot2::position_dodge(.8)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.3, position = ggplot2::position_dodge(.8)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Number of columns", y = "Milliseconds per call (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    ggplot2::guides(colour = ggplot2::guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))
}

Figure 12 shows how the QR interface timings change as the number of columns grows. The two recursive block choices reveal the effect of partitioning the calculation, while the compact base-R output provides a separate interface-level comparison. Differences between these curves therefore reflect both computational methods and the representation returned.

benchmark_plot("QR")

Figure 12: QR interface timings across column dimensions. Compact and explicit outputs are distinguished in the legend. Designs have 500 rows; each setting uses 5 timed repetitions.

At the largest tested dimension (p = 80), the smallest median time is 0.547 milliseconds per call for fastQR, nb = p/2. Changing the block size changes the balance between panel factorization and matrix operations, so the preferred choice can depend on matrix dimensions and the linear-algebra library. The compact base-R result and explicit fastQR factors remain different deliverables.

The triangular-factor workload in Figure 13 separates the cost of factorizing an available cross-product matrix from the cost of first forming it. This distinction matters when deciding whether a timing is relevant to a calculation that starts from the observations themselves.

benchmark_plot("Cholesky")

Figure 13: Triangular-factor timings, with separate baselines for an available Gram matrix and for its formation from X. Designs have 500 rows; each setting uses 5 timed repetitions.

At the largest tested dimension (p = 80), the smallest median time is 0.061 milliseconds per call for chol, Gram available. The two Cholesky baselines separate factorization from the cost of forming the Gram matrix. Compare qrchol with crossprod + chol when starting from the design alone; chol, Gram available is relevant when that matrix has already been computed. Their numerical-stability implications also differ because explicitly forming the Gram matrix squares the condition number.

Figure 14 isolates the solution stage for a shared, precomputed system. Data preparation and formation of the cross-products have already taken place. The comparison therefore measures the work of the displayed solver calls, with solution accuracy checked independently in the preceding validation table.

benchmark_plot("Solve")

Figure 14: Solution times for the same precomputed normal-equation system. Designs have 500 rows; each setting uses 5 timed repetitions.

At the largest tested dimension (p = 80), the smallest median time is 0.111 milliseconds per call for base qr.solve. Both solvers start from the same precomputed normal-equation system. The differences therefore concern the solution stage, not preprocessing or prediction. The validation table checks agreement separately from execution time; a faster call would not be useful if it failed that check.

The normal-equation workload squares the condition number of the design, as discussed above. Good agreement on these random examples does not remove that limitation. The supplied large-grid option can be computationally expensive; the small default run supplies reproducible examples, not evidence of performance at untested dimensions. No historical cached measurements are mixed with these newly computed results.

6.5 Matched comparisons with unpivoted LAPACK

The following experiment separates the factorization algorithm from the representation requested by its caller. A small R interface calls the LAPACK routines linked to this R installation: DGEQRF computes compact Householder factors, and DORGQR forms an explicit orthogonal factor. No column pivoting is performed in these two routines. Comparing their thin output with fastQR’s thin output therefore avoids conflating pivoting or deferred construction of Q with the factorization itself.

The recorded run uses 4 shapes, with 300 or 600 rows and 20 or 60 columns, and 5 timed repetitions after warm-up. Each repetition uses a calibrated batch; the numbers below are median milliseconds per call. Compilation, random-data generation, numerical validation and plotting lie outside the timed regions. The R interfaces and their allocations are included. These measurements describe this machine and these shapes, rather than a universal ranking of implementations.

initial_medians <- aggregate(seconds ~ n + p + workload + method, initial_lapack, median)
largest_thin <- subset(initial_medians, workload == "thin_unpivoted" & n == max(n) & p == max(p))
base_thin_seconds <- largest_thin$seconds[largest_thin$method == "LAPACK DGEQRF + DORGQR"]
largest_thin$milliseconds <- 1000 * largest_thin$seconds
largest_thin$LAPACK_over_method <- base_thin_seconds / largest_thin$seconds
knitr::kable(largest_thin[, c("n", "p", "method", "milliseconds", "LAPACK_over_method")],
             digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Thin Q and R for the same largest design. A time ratio above one favors the named method over LAPACK.")
Thin Q and R for the same largest design. A time ratio above one favors the named method over LAPACK.

600 60 fastQR thin recursive 0.6875 1.1591 
largest_R <- subset(initial_medians, workload == "R_unpivoted" & n == max(n) & p == max(p))
base_R_seconds <- largest_R$seconds[largest_R$method == "LAPACK DGEQRF + extract R"]
largest_R$milliseconds <- 1000 * largest_R$seconds
largest_R$LAPACK_over_method <- base_R_seconds / largest_R$seconds
knitr::kable(largest_R[, c("n", "p", "method", "milliseconds", "LAPACK_over_method")],
             digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Triangular-factor-only requests on the same design, with no explicit Q returned.")

The distinction between qr_thin(), the direct Householder implementation and the recursive implementation matters: qr_thin() now uses an internal LAPACK backend, while the recursive implementation combines LAPACK panels with dense products. They perform different matrix operations even though all return a thin factorization. Likewise, an R-only interface should be compared with extracting R from a LAPACK factorization, rather than with a call that also forms Q. The complete raw results retain every shape and repetition.

Figure 15 compares calls that all return explicit thin factors for the same matrix. The logarithmic time axis keeps the faster and slower implementations visible within a single display. The repeated measurements describe timing variation on this fixed problem, rather than variation across independently generated datasets.

plot_lapack <- subset(initial_lapack, workload == "thin_unpivoted" & n == max(n) & p == max(p))
ggplot2::ggplot(plot_lapack, ggplot2::aes(x = seconds * 1000, y = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, colour = "#526070") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#b5121b", size = 1.5) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Milliseconds per call (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

Figure 15: Thin-factor timings for a 600 by 60 design. Each point represents one calibrated repetition; elapsed time is shown on a logarithmic scale, with lower values indicating faster calls.

The calls in Figure 15 return the same thin representation. For an update, the starting factors already exist, so the relevant alternative is recomputing the factors after the change. The next table keeps R-only and explicit thin-QR requests separate. The initial factors are excluded from these single-operation times; maintaining a full input Q still has a storage cost even when the requested result is thin.

modification_medians <- aggregate(seconds ~ operation + workload + method, modifications_lapack, median)
matched_updates <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(modification_medians,
  interaction(modification_medians$operation, modification_medians$workload, drop = TRUE)), function(z) {
    lapack <- grepl("LAPACK", z$method)
    data.frame(operation = gsub("_", " ", z$operation[1]), workload = z$workload[1],
      fastQR_ms = 1000 * z$seconds[!lapack], LAPACK_ms = 1000 * z$seconds[lapack],
      LAPACK_over_fastQR = z$seconds[lapack] / z$seconds[!lapack])
}))

An advantage for updating R does not imply the same advantage for updating explicit QR factors, nor does it establish an advantage for an initial factorization. The appropriate choice depends on whether the factors already exist and whether subsequent calculations need Q. The downloadable benchmark archive contains the R driver, the unpivoted LAPACK adapter and the raw timings, allowing these comparisons to be rerun on another machine.

6.6 Ridge updates: accuracy and speed on tall and wide designs

The ridge experiments provide a statistical application in which retaining a triangular factor has a measured computational advantage, including when the observed design has more columns than rows. The chapter Ridge regression as the design grows gives the augmented-design construction and the complete workflow. Here we collect its final numerical comparisons alongside the other timing results, so the statistical application can be assessed under the same reporting conventions.

Both workflows return the updated ridge coefficients through an R-only solve and account for the response cross-product. The starting factorization is available to the update but is excluded from both single-change timing measurements. Recomputing uses a fresh unpivoted LAPACK factorization of the augmented design. The table shows median milliseconds per call from five calibrated repetitions, including each workflow’s required matrix construction and triangular solves.

final_ridge_results <- read.csv(file.path(lapack_root, "results/bench_ridge_summary.csv"))
knitr::kable(final_ridge_results, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
 caption = "Final ridge comparison for additions of ten observations or five predictors. Speedup is recomputation time divided by updating time; values above one favor updating.")

For the design with 300 observations and 450 predictors, updating after the addition of ten observations takes 2.69 ms, compared with 6.00 ms for recomputation, a speed advantage of 2.23 times. Adding five predictors takes 2.44 ms with updating and 5.87 ms with recomputation, a speed advantage of 2.41 times. Both comparisons hold the total penalty \(\alpha\) fixed and produce the same target ridge fit. They demonstrate a measured benefit from reusing the existing factor and response information, including when \(p>n\).

Figure 16 makes the size and direction of the time advantage explicit. At fixed total penalty, the measured observation and predictor updates are faster than rebuilding the augmented factor in these settings. Keeping the normalized penalty fixed is a different workload: adding observations changes the penalty block as well, and the construction used here is slower for the wide designs. The figure retains that case rather than transferring a fixed-total-penalty advantage to a different optimization problem.

final_ridge_results$design <- paste0("n = ", final_ridge_results$n, ", p = ", final_ridge_results$p)
final_ridge_results$operation_label <- factor(final_ridge_results$operation,
 levels = c("columns_fixed_alpha", "rows_fixed_alpha", "rows_fixed_lambda"),
 labels = c("Add predictors: fixed total penalty", "Add observations: fixed total penalty",
            "Add observations: fixed normalized penalty"))
ggplot2::ggplot(final_ridge_results, ggplot2::aes(speedup, design)) +
 ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
 ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#b5121b", size = 2) +
 ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~operation_label, ncol = 1) +
 ggplot2::labs(x = "Recomputation time / updating time (log scale)", y = NULL) +
 ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

Figure 16: Ridge updating speed relative to refactorization on the same target fit. Values to the right of one favor updating. Panels distinguish predictor additions at fixed total penalty, observation additions at fixed total penalty, and observation additions at fixed normalized penalty; all cases are retained.

The time comparison is accompanied by independent numerical validation. Across these fits, the largest scaled coefficient or prediction discrepancy from the orthogonal augmented-QR reference is 7.29e-15. These checks support the reported examples; they do not establish stability for arbitrarily small penalties or a universal timing ranking. In particular, the comparison maintains a primal triangular factor of size \(p\) by \(p\). A dual formulation can be attractive when \(p\) is much larger than \(n\), and is a different computational alternative from the update-versus-recompute question measured here.

7 Mathematical background and further reading

The computational ideas in this guide build on standard orthogonal factorizations and their modification after changes to a matrix. For full treatments, see Golub and Van Loan (2013) and Björck (2015); for least-squares algorithms, see Björck (2024). The package authors develop updating methods and statistical applications in Bernardi, Busatto, and Cattelan (2024).

7.1 Why orthogonal transformations?

Consider the full-column-rank least-squares problem \[ \widehat\beta=\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}\|y-Xb\|_2^2, \qquad X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p},\quad y\in\mathbb R^n,\quad n\ge p. \] The thin factorization \(X=Q_1R_1\) separates an orthonormal basis \(Q_1\) for the column space from the coordinates stored in the triangular matrix \(R_1\). Complete that basis to \(Q=[Q_1,Q_2]\), so that \(Q^\top Q=I_n\). Orthogonal multiplication preserves Euclidean length, and \[ Q^\top(y-Xb) =\begin{pmatrix}Q_1^\top y-R_1b\\Q_2^\top y\end{pmatrix}. \] Taking squared lengths gives \[ \|y-Xb\|_2^2 =\|Q_1^\top y-R_1b\|_2^2+\|Q_2^\top y\|_2^2. \] The second term is unchanged when \(b\) changes. Because \(R_1\) is nonsingular, the first term can be made zero by solving \[ c=Q_1^\top y\in\mathbb R^p, \qquad R_1\widehat\beta=c. \] These are the two computational stages of a direct QR least-squares solve: project the response onto the orthonormal basis, then recover its coordinates relative to the original columns of \(X\). In R, the projection is crossprod(Q1, y) and the triangular solution is backsolve(R1, c). No inverse of \(R_1\) is formed.

The triangular structure determines the order of the solve. The last equation gives \(\widehat\beta_p=c_p/r_{pp}\); the preceding equations are recovered backwards through \[ \widehat\beta_j =\frac{c_j-\sum_{k=j+1}^p r_{jk}\widehat\beta_k}{r_{jj}}, \qquad j=p-1,\ldots,1. \] The nonzero diagonal entries required here follow from full column rank. The fitted response and residual are \[ \widehat y=Q_1Q_1^\top y, \qquad e=y-\widehat y=(I_n-Q_1Q_1^\top)y. \] Thus \(Q_1^\top e=0\): the residual is orthogonal to every direction used to construct the fit. This identity supplies a useful numerical check in addition to agreement between coefficient vectors.

If only \(R_1\) and \(h=X^\top y\) are retained, the same coefficients follow from \(R_1^\top R_1\widehat\beta=h\). The calculation then requires a forward solve followed by a backward solve, \[ R_1^\top z=h,\qquad R_1\widehat\beta=z. \] In exact arithmetic, \(z=Q_1^\top y\), since \(X^\top y=R_1^\top Q_1^\top y\). This relation explains why an R-only representation can support regression, and why the right-hand side has to be maintained alongside the factor. The numerical consequences of forming cross-products are examined in the accuracy chapter (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2024).

7.2 Classical and modified Gram–Schmidt

Let \(X=[x_1,\ldots,x_p]\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) have linearly independent columns, with \(n\geq p\). Classical Gram–Schmidt constructs an orthonormal basis for their span. At step \(k\), set \[ \begin{aligned} r_{jk}&=q_j^\top x_k\quad(j<k),\\ v_k&=x_k-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}r_{jk}q_j,\\ r_{kk}&=\|v_k\|_2,\qquad q_k=v_k/r_{kk}. \end{aligned} \] The empty sum at \(k=1\) is zero. Full column rank ensures \(r_{kk}>0\) in exact arithmetic. With \(r_{jk}=0\) for \(j>k\), these identities give \(X=QR\) and \(Q^\top Q=I_p\). The temporary residual \(v_k\) is distinct from the normalized vector \(q_k\).

Modified Gram–Schmidt instead starts with \(v=x_k\) and, for \(j=1,\ldots,k-1\), successively computes \[ r_{jk}=q_j^\top v,\qquad v\leftarrow v-r_{jk}q_j; \] it then sets \(r_{kk}=\|v\|_2\) and \(q_k=v/r_{kk}\). The two algorithms are equivalent in exact arithmetic, but their floating-point behavior differs: computing projections from the updated residual generally reduces loss of orthogonality. Reorthogonalization may still be needed for difficult problems (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2015).

At each step, the inner products describe the part of the current column already explained by the existing basis. Subtracting those components leaves a residual direction; normalizing that residual supplies the next basis vector. The recorded coefficients give the identity \(x_k=\sum_{j\le k}q_jr_{jk}\), so the construction produces both factors rather than Q alone.

The following educational implementation follows the modified scheme. Its diagonal check detects a residual that is too small relative to the input column to normalize reliably. That check is useful for understanding the algorithm, but it is not a general rank-revealing procedure. The example checks reconstruction and orthogonality separately on a well-conditioned design.

mgs <- function(X) {
  n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X)
  Q <- matrix(0, n, p); R <- matrix(0, p, p)
  for (k in seq_len(p)) {
    v <- X[, k]
    if (k > 1L) for (j in seq_len(k - 1L)) {
      R[j, k] <- sum(Q[, j] * v)
      v <- v - R[j, k] * Q[, j]
    }
    R[k, k] <- sqrt(sum(v^2))
    if (R[k, k] <= .Machine$double.eps * sqrt(sum(X[, k]^2)))
      stop("Numerically dependent column: use a rank-revealing factorization.")
    Q[, k] <- v / R[k, k]
  }
  list(Q = Q, R = R)
}
set.seed(2040)
X_gs <- matrix(rnorm(80 * 8), 80, 8)
gs <- mgs(X_gs)
gs_checks <- c(reconstruction = norm(X_gs - gs$Q %*% gs$R, "F") / norm(X_gs, "F"),
               orthogonality = norm(crossprod(gs$Q) - diag(8), "F"))
gs_checks
## reconstruction  orthogonality 
##   1.154784e-16   1.019128e-15
stopifnot(max(gs_checks) < 1e-10)

7.3 Householder transformations and Givens rotations

Gram–Schmidt constructs basis vectors by successive projections. Householder QR instead transforms the matrix into triangular form using reflections. For a nonzero vector \(v\), the matrix \[ H=I-2vv^\top/(v^\top v) \] is symmetric and satisfies \(H^\top H=I\). For a column segment \(x\), a reflector can be chosen so that \(Hx=\alpha e_1\), eliminating every entry of that segment except its first. Applying such a transformation to successive trailing submatrices removes the entries below the diagonal without changing Euclidean lengths.

If the embedded reflections satisfy \(H_s\cdots H_1X=R\), then \[ X=QR,\qquad Q=H_1\cdots H_s, \] with the full or thin factors selected as required. Each reflection is represented by a vector and a coefficient, so its action can be applied without storing a dense matrix H. Compact Householder output retains that information. Forming Q, multiplying by Q and multiplying by its transpose are related operations, but need not incur the same storage cost.

A Givens rotation acts on just two coordinates. With \[ G=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix},\qquad c^2+s^2=1, \] choosing \(c=a/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and \(s=b/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) gives \[ G\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\\0\end{pmatrix} \] when \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\). Implementations compute the rotation parameters with appropriate numerical safeguards. Because a rotation changes only a pair of coordinates, a sequence of rotations can restore triangular form after a local insertion or deletion.

Both constructions use orthogonal transformations to control the propagation of rounding error. They do not remove sensitivity already present in a nearly singular design. The distinction between an accurate factorization and an accurate coefficient vector is therefore retained throughout the numerical experiments (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2015).

7.4 What a row update changes

Suppose \(X=Q_1R_1\) has already been computed and a batch of \(m\) observations is represented by \(U^\top\), where \(U\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}\). The enlarged design is \[ X_+=\begin{pmatrix}X\\U^\top\end{pmatrix}. \] Applying the previously available orthogonal transformation to the original observation block reduces the new factorization problem to triangularizing \[ \begin{pmatrix}R_1\\U^\top\end{pmatrix} \in\mathbb R^{(p+m)\times p}, \] together with zero rows that do not affect the triangular factor. The new observations have to be incorporated, but the original n-row design need not be factorized again to obtain R.

The corresponding cross-product identity is \[ X_+^\top X_+=R_1^\top R_1+UU^\top. \] It also explains what additional information a regression update needs. If \(y_+\) is the vector of responses for the new batch, the right-hand side becomes \(h_+=h+Uy_+\), where \(h=X^\top y\). Updating R alone does not update that response-dependent quantity.

Deleting observations reverses the signs in both updates. The resulting cross-product matrix is positive semidefinite when the deleted rows belong to the original design; it is positive definite precisely when the remaining design has full column rank. A downdated factor may still represent a rank-deficient design, but the unpivoted triangular coefficient solve then requires further treatment. Near a loss of rank, cancellation in the subtraction makes the numerical checks especially important.

7.5 Ridge as augmented least squares

For the normalized ridge criterion used in the regression chapter, define the augmented response and design by \[ \widetilde y=\begin{pmatrix}y\\0_p\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{n+p},\qquad \widetilde X=\begin{pmatrix}X\\\sqrt{n\lambda}I_p\end{pmatrix} \in\mathbb R^{(n+p)\times p}. \] The \(p\) additional entries of \(\widetilde y\) are zero, and the \(p\) additional rows of \(\widetilde X\) encode the penalty. For \(b\in\mathbb R^p\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \|\widetilde y-\widetilde Xb\|_2^2 &=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}y-Xb\\-\sqrt{n\lambda}b\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2^2\\ &=\|y-Xb\|_2^2+n\lambda\|b\|_2^2. \end{aligned} \] Multiplying the normalized criterion by n does not change its minimizer, so the ridge estimate is the ordinary least-squares solution for these augmented data. With a thin factorization \(\widetilde X=\widetilde Q_1\widetilde R_1\), it can be computed by \[ \widetilde R_1\widehat\beta_\lambda =\widetilde Q_1^\top\widetilde y. \] Equivalently, differentiating the original criterion gives \[ (X^\top X+n\lambda I_p)\widehat\beta_\lambda=X^\top y. \] The extra rows imply \(\widetilde R_1^\top\widetilde R_1=X^\top X+n\lambda I_p\). An R-only calculation therefore uses this factor in two triangular solves, just as in the unpenalized case. A positive penalty makes the system positive definite even when X has dependent columns, although a particular fitting interface can impose additional restrictions on input dimensions.

The augmented formulation is an independent way to check the implementations. It also identifies the scale of the penalty: the factor n is a consequence of dividing the data loss by n. Within cross-validation, n is replaced by the size of the corresponding training set.

The intercept is handled separately in the ridge tutorial by centering. If a column of ones were simply included in the penalized design, that coefficient would also be penalized. Predictor means and scales must be estimated again within each cross-validation training fold.

7.6 Choosing a representation

The representation should retain the information needed by the next calculation. A compact factorization stores the transformations defining Q and is useful when only their action on vectors is required. Thin factors make the column-space basis explicit, supporting projections and direct QR solves. A full factorization also retains an orthogonal complement, which is used by some update routines but can require substantially more storage for a tall design.

An R-only representation is sufficient when subsequent operations need the cross-product information \(R^\top R\) and triangular solves. Regression still requires a compatible right-hand side such as \(X^\top y\), and insertion of new predictors can require cross-products with their observed values. These requirements distinguish the information needed by the algorithm from the matrix finally returned to R.

The examples use reconstruction identities, independent coefficient calculations and recorded timings to examine those choices. The function guide describes the interfaces, while the numerical experiments show how representation, conditioning and the starting information affect the computation.
